title: Paula Poundstone
location: Buskirk-Chumley Theater,114 East Kirkwood Avenue, Bloomington, IN 47408, USA
description:
Iconic comedian Paula Poundstone is known for her smart, observational humor and a spontaneous wit that has become the stuff of legend. She regularly plays theaters across the country, hosts a weekly comedy podcast, Nobody Listens to Paula Poundstone, and is a regular panelist on NPR’s Wait, Wait… Don’t Tell Me. She also voiced the character ‘Forgetter Paula’ in the feature films Inside Out and Inside Out 2.

Paula has starred in several HBO specials, including Cats, Cops and Stuff, which nabbed a cable ACE award for Best Comedy Special. She was the first female comic to host the White House Correspondents Dinner. She filmed live coverage of the 1992 Democratic and Republican National Conventions and the Presidential Inaugural for The Tonight Show with Jay Leno and at the 93rd Emmy Awards. Paula has starred in two television series, both entitled The Paula Poundstone Show.

Paula’s second book, The Totally Unscientific Study of the Search for Human Happiness, was one of eight semi-finalists for the Thurber Prize for American Humor; the audiobook was one of five finalists for the AUDIE award for Audiobook of the Year.

Paula has released five albums and is featured in several documentaries and compendiums noting influential comedians of our time.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Osamu James Nakagawa: TRACE | Exhibition
location: FAR Center for Contemporary Arts, 202 S. Rogers St., Bloomington, IN 47404
description: Opening reception and artist talk: Friday, September 4, 58 pm  Nakagawa combines photographs taken at the sites of Japanese-American incarceration camps with photograms of found objects and rubbings of the memorials.  Using diptychs, Nakagawa pairs the past and the present, flattening the boundaries between them. TRACE seeks to reveal what can't be seen anymore, things that happened eighty years ago and have been quietly buried. Through a direct and immersive process, using actual objects and surfaces from the sites, Nakagawa unearths this history of forced incarceration.About the artist:  Osamu James Nakagawa was born in New York City in 1962, raised in Tokyo, and then returned to the US at the age of 15. He is the Distinguished Professor and the Ruth N. Halls Professor of Photography at Indiana University. Nakagawa is a recipient of the 2010 Guggenheim Fellowship, the 2010 Higashikawa New Photographer of the Year and 2015 Sagamihara Photographer of the Year in Japan.  Nakagawa's work has been exhibited internationally, selected solo exhibitions include PGI, Tokyo; Kyoto University of the Arts; Sepia EYE, New York; Sakima Art Museum, Okinawa, Japan; and others. Group shows include "A Shared Elegy" with Emmet Gowin and Elijah Gowin; and "After Photoshop" at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. His work is included in numerous public collections, including George Eastman Museum and the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum.  Link to the artist's website:https://jamesnakagawa.com/en (https://jamesnakagawa.com/en)  FAR Center for Contemporary Arts:https://thefar.org/events/event/121689 (https://thefar.org/events/event/121689)
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: National Drive Electric Month at Community Farmer's Market
description:
At the Bloomington Community Farmers’ Market, we’re excited to welcome neighbors, families, and curious visitors to stop by and learn more about the growing world of electric transportation. Our booth will be hosted by the newly reformed Hoosier Electric Vehicle Association in Bloomington, reconnecting EV owners, supporters, and anyone interested in cleaner, quieter ways to get around our community. The market takes place at Showers Common next to City Hall, a familiar gathering place where Bloomington comes together every week to shop, talk, and share ideas. And don't forget A Fair of the Arts is also happening.

We’ll have friendly, straightforward information about electric vehicles, hybrids, electric bikes, and the practical benefits of making transportation more efficient and more sustainable. Whether you’re already driving electric, thinking about your next vehicle, or just curious about how EVs fit into everyday life in Bloomington, we’d love for you to stop by, ask questions, and join the conversation. If we have an electric bike on hand, it will be a great way to see another side of local electric mobility up close.

title: Bloomington Community Farmers' Market
location: Showers Common, 402 N Morton Street, Bloomington, IN 47404
description:
The Bloomington Community Farmers' Market takes place rain or shine every Saturday, April through October, at Showers Common next to City Hall, 401 N. Morton St. in Bloomington.
 April-September: 8 a.m.-12:30 p.m.
October: 9 a.m.-12:30 p.m.
 November: 9 a.m.-12:30 p.m. at the Pavilion at Switchyard Park 
 Nestled in picturesque downtown charm, the Bloomington Community Farmers' Market is a vital part of the local food culture. 
 Market goers can expect to find a wide assortment of goods from the farm and field, including fruits and vegetables, eggs, meats and cheeses, honey, seasonal flowers, and annual and perennial plants. Food and beverage artisans provide a tasteful variety of satisfying breads, drinks, pastries, and savory dishes. This weekly gathering provides individuals the opportunity to connect with their community in meaningful ways while supporting small farmers and businesses.

title: 17th Annual Great Glass Pumpkin Patch
location: Monroe County Courthouse Lawn, 100 W. Kirkwood Avenue, Bloomington, IN 47403
description:
Every October, we celebrate the season with over 1,000 stunning blown glass pumpkins displayed for sale on the Bloomington Courthouse Lawn. The enchanting atmosphere, complete with crisp autumn air and glass sparkling in the sun on haybales, is one pumpkin spice latte away from a hallmark movie. Crafted by our talented glassblowing apprentices, each pumpkin is a unique masterpiece, hand-made with care and artistry. 
These exquisite creations are not just a feast for the eyes though; they also play a crucial role in supporting our mission here at BCGC. The Great Glass Pumpkin Patch is our largest fundraiser of the year, and it also allows us an opportunity to teach glassblowing skills to our apprentices at low cost.
We hope you are able to join us at our next Great Glass Pumpkin Patch and that you find a perfect pumpkin to take home with you!
 Pumpkin Preview- Saturday, September 26th, 6-8 pm, at BCGC
 Pumpkin Patch - Saturday, October 10th, 10 am - 3 pm (or until the pumpkins are gone!), at the Bloomington Courthouse

title: Bloomington Blues & Boogie Woogie Piano Festival
description:
Presented by Bloomington Boogies
On October 10-12, 2026, enjoy acclaimed artists at Bloomington Boogies: The Bloomington Blues & Boogie Woogie Piano Festival. Featuring musicians who play boogie-woogie, blues, and related styles in free and ticketed performances, the festival was voted a top 10 festival in Indiana. Bloomington Boogies strives to introduce young people to artists and various non-classical styles through public concerts and free educational activities, including school performances, workshops, and master classes.
 The festival begins with free performances throughout the day Saturday, Oct. 10th:
• 11 a.m., Monroe County History Center, 202 E. 6th St., Bloomington - WFHB's "Saturday's Child" will feature pianists Yoshi "Z2"Tsuji and Rob Rio 
• 2 p.m., also at the History Center - multi-instrumentalist Deanna Bogart presents performance/workshop "Inside the Groove: Blues, Boogie-Woogie & Improvisation." Youth and aspiring pianists are invited; pre-registration required, beginning Sept. 1 at the festival's Education page - https://bloomingtonboogies.com/education, limited to 75 people.
• 5 p.m., John Waldron Arts Center, 122 S. Walnut St., Bloomington - pianist Dr. Keith McCutchen will present "A Tribute to Three Entities: Blues, Gospel, and Jazz Piano”; pre-registration required, beginning Sept. 1 at the Education page, limited to 60 people.
• 8 p.m., Cardinal Spirits, 922 S. Morton St., Bloomington - accordionist Bruce "Sunpie" Barnes, guitarist Matt Hampsey, and special guest pianist Silvan Zingg.
 On Sunday, Oct. 11, the Bloomington Boogies 2026 Festival Concert takes place at the Buskirk-Chumley Theater, 114 E. Kirkwood Ave., beginning at 3 p.m. Tickets are required, and may be purchased in advance at the Buskirk-Chumley Theater Box Office, 114 E. Kirkwood Ave., Bloomington, IN, by phone at 812-323-3020, or at buskirkchumley.org. General admission in advance for adults is $34; $24 for under age 12, plus handling fees. Food and beverages will be available.
 Artists performing and or presenting workshops at festival events are coming from far and wide:
• Rob Rio - Boogie-woogie/blues piano from Los Angeles
• Jason Marsalis - Jazz/blues vibraphone/drums from New Orleans
• Deanna Bogart - Blues/boogie-woogie piano/sax from Palm Desert, CA
• "Sunpie" Barnes & Matt Hampsey - Zydeco/blues accordion and guitar from New Orleans

• Concert lineup subject to change
 More free events continue Monday, Oct. 12th:

Eagleson Avenue, Bloomington, IN 47405; register at the Education page. 
• Zoe Imani Shepard will present a free workshop on jazz violin: “Jazz Improvisation 101 for String Players" at 4:30 p.m. at Fairview Elementary School, 500 W 7th St, Bloomington, IN 47404; register at the Education page. 
• Tri-North and Jackson Creek Middle Schools and Fairview and Templeton Elementary Schools will all enjoy free concerts by guest artists; school concerts are for students, faculty, staff, and invited guests.

title: Discardia Mending Day
location: Monroe County Public Library - Downtown, 303 E Kirkwood Ave, Bloomington, IN 47408, USA
description: Mending Day is the second Saturday of each month, noon till 4PM. Join our sewing circle as we teach, learn, help others, mend and create art.Please be kind and pre-launder your projects.Bring your sewing, interest in sewing, interest to learn, and willingness to teach, or just bring pre-washed fabric items in need of mending or alteration! We fix and alter garments and other fabric items for free, as a service to the greater community, for fun! Let’s keep things useful and out of landfill together!Calling all Artists, Fashion Designers, Creatives, and Community Members of All Ages Interested in Sustainable Practices. Discardia, a program of the Center for Sustainable Living, creates an environment for local designers to brainstorm to make upcycled clothing and to teach people in the community how to upcycle their own items. Get involved with Discardia as a Mending Day Sewing Advisor: https://www.bloomingtonvolunteernetwork.org/need/detail/?need_id=355829Discardia members and volunteer Sewing Advisors assist attendees in mending clothing, giving them an opportunity to learn how to sew or work on any other project involving clothing. Sewing machines and basic supplies are provided to participants, for free, and all ages are welcome!Volunteer Sewing Advisors offer help to participants with altering or repairing the garments that they have brought in. Use your skills to assist participants with creative solutions, but not to make all the decisions for them.Help is also appreciated in setting up and tearing down before and after the event (30 minutes each). This is a great way to empower as well as collaborate with a group of creative problem solvers and learn to use the various tools and tricks of the trade to make it easier to make adjustments to our own clothes so that they fit well and are comfortable and we feel good wearing them.All skill levels are welcome and training is provided. It's a lot of fun and makes you feel empowered and confident. Contact Stephen Hale, Discardia Project Manager if interested at 812-334-0922.

title: Future Tense 2026
location: Grunwald Gallery of Art, 1201 E. 7th Street, Fine Arts Building, Bloomington, IN 47405
description:
The Grunwald Gallery of Art at Indiana University Bloomington partners with Surface Design Association to present "Future Tense 2026"—a national student exhibition juried by José Santiago Pérez. Since 2017, Surface Design Association (SDA) has invited students to submit work for the annual Juried Student Exhibition. The ninth iteration of this exhibition will be held at Indiana University’s Grunwald Gallery of Art in Bloomington, IN from August 25-October 31, 2026. Exhibiting artists are eligible for four awards recognizing excellence in artistic practice. 
"Future Tense” celebrates the creative work of student artists, designers, and makers working with, or inspired by fiber, or textile materials, or techniques. This exhibition offers a glimpse into the future of contemporary fibers by presenting the very best work being made by students in the field today.

title: ARTIST'S TALK & DEMO: JONATHAN NASH
location: Juniper Art Gallery, 615 w. Kirkwood Ave., Bloomington, IN 47404
description:
Our featured artist for the month of October, Jonathan Nash, will talk about his exhibit, Bound by Nature. This commissioned series of twenty original Art Nouveau-inspired illustrations created for the wedding of Erica Nadolkski and Jordan Evans.
Jonathan will talk about his technique and inspirations, as well as provide a demonstration of his material and style.
More info: Each poster celebrates a different insect personally selected by the bride, pairing it with native flora and elements of its natural habitat. Drawing inspiration from vintage natural history plates and the decorative compositions of the Art Nouveau movement, every illustration is framed by ornamental motifs unique to its featured species, incorporating elements from its life cycle, host plants, and surrounding ecosystem.
Originally designed as table markers for the couple’s wedding reception, the complete series extends beyond its ceremonial purpose as a celebration of transformation, growth, and the interconnectedness of nature. Like marriage itself, metamorphosis is a process of continual change. Reflected throughout the lives of the insects depicted in these illustrations.
Following the wedding, the collection will be exhibited at Juniper Gallery in October as a complete body of work with reproductions available.

title: Kyle Kinane's Triumphant Return to Bloomington!
location: The Comedy Attic, 123 S Walnut Street, Bloomington, IN
description: Kyle Kinane is a comedian from Addison, Illinois. According to Wikipedia, he is a notable person from that town. Other notable residents of Addison have been the boxer Leon Spinks and a woman who wrote poetry about Beanie Babies. Raised in such a cultural fondue pot as this, it was natural for Kyle to find his way from warehouse work into show business. As a comedian, he has been seen on The Tonight Show, Netflix’s “The Standups,” and 5 of his own hour-length specials . As an actor, he’s been in the Judd Apatow series “Love” and truTV’s “Those Who Can’t.” He was also on “Drunk History,” where he unfortunately wasn’t acting. As a voice over actor, he was the former voice of Comedy Central for 8 years and currently plays Bullet on the Netflix series “Paradise PD.” He is also co-host of the No Accounting for Taste podcast along with Shane Torres. As a musician, he has done nothing, as he is not a musician. Kyle’s most recent standup work, “Dirt Nap,” was recorded at Acme Comedy Club in Minneapolis, Minnesota and was released in April of 2024.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Osamu James Nakagawa: TRACE | Exhibition
location: FAR Center for Contemporary Arts, 202 S. Rogers St., Bloomington, IN 47404
description: Opening reception and artist talk: Friday, September 4, 58 pm  Nakagawa combines photographs taken at the sites of Japanese-American incarceration camps with photograms of found objects and rubbings of the memorials.  Using diptychs, Nakagawa pairs the past and the present, flattening the boundaries between them. TRACE seeks to reveal what can't be seen anymore, things that happened eighty years ago and have been quietly buried. Through a direct and immersive process, using actual objects and surfaces from the sites, Nakagawa unearths this history of forced incarceration.About the artist:  Osamu James Nakagawa was born in New York City in 1962, raised in Tokyo, and then returned to the US at the age of 15. He is the Distinguished Professor and the Ruth N. Halls Professor of Photography at Indiana University. Nakagawa is a recipient of the 2010 Guggenheim Fellowship, the 2010 Higashikawa New Photographer of the Year and 2015 Sagamihara Photographer of the Year in Japan.  Nakagawa's work has been exhibited internationally, selected solo exhibitions include PGI, Tokyo; Kyoto University of the Arts; Sepia EYE, New York; Sakima Art Museum, Okinawa, Japan; and others. Group shows include "A Shared Elegy" with Emmet Gowin and Elijah Gowin; and "After Photoshop" at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. His work is included in numerous public collections, including George Eastman Museum and the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum.  Link to the artist's website:https://jamesnakagawa.com/en (https://jamesnakagawa.com/en)  FAR Center for Contemporary Arts:https://thefar.org/events/event/121689 (https://thefar.org/events/event/121689)
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Memory Transformed Symposium: Materials of Heritage in Jewish Eastern European Life
description: Join the Borns Jewish Studies Program for the opening symposium of Memory Transformed: Materials of Heritage in Jewish Eastern European Life, a day of scholarship, art, and music exploring how Eastern European Jewish culture is remembered and continues to shape contemporary artistic production.11:00 a.m. — Complimentary Brunch at the Tudor Room*The complimentary brunch at the Tudor Room is currently at capacity. If space becomes available, registered attendees will be contacted.*12:30–3:00 p.m. — SymposiumDogwood Room, Indiana Memorial Union  The symposium will feature two panels examining Jewish material culture, music, memory, and the cultural afterlives of objects associated with Eastern European Jewish life. title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).

title: Osamu James Nakagawa: TRACE | Exhibition
location: FAR Center for Contemporary Arts, 202 S. Rogers St., Bloomington, IN 47404
description: Opening reception and artist talk: Friday, September 4, 58 pm  Nakagawa combines photographs taken at the sites of Japanese-American incarceration camps with photograms of found objects and rubbings of the memorials.  Using diptychs, Nakagawa pairs the past and the present, flattening the boundaries between them. TRACE seeks to reveal what can't be seen anymore, things that happened eighty years ago and have been quietly buried. Through a direct and immersive process, using actual objects and surfaces from the sites, Nakagawa unearths this history of forced incarceration.About the artist:  Osamu James Nakagawa was born in New York City in 1962, raised in Tokyo, and then returned to the US at the age of 15. He is the Distinguished Professor and the Ruth N. Halls Professor of Photography at Indiana University. Nakagawa is a recipient of the 2010 Guggenheim Fellowship, the 2010 Higashikawa New Photographer of the Year and 2015 Sagamihara Photographer of the Year in Japan.  Nakagawa's work has been exhibited internationally, selected solo exhibitions include PGI, Tokyo; Kyoto University of the Arts; Sepia EYE, New York; Sakima Art Museum, Okinawa, Japan; and others. Group shows include "A Shared Elegy" with Emmet Gowin and Elijah Gowin; and "After Photoshop" at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. His work is included in numerous public collections, including George Eastman Museum and the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum.  Link to the artist's website:https://jamesnakagawa.com/en (https://jamesnakagawa.com/en)  FAR Center for Contemporary Arts:https://thefar.org/events/event/121689 (https://thefar.org/events/event/121689)

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Be a Part of the"Day in My Life"Series
Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.

title: Center for Refugee Studies Op-Ed Initiative Webinar Series
description: The CRS Op-Ed Initiative, open to faculty, students, and the CRS community, teaches participants how to convert research insights into accessible, public-facing op-eds. This four-course series covers how to develop, write, edit, and publish op-eds, and why opinion writing is an important vessel for spreading innovative ideas and sparking important discussions. Participants do not need any prior publication experience to join, and the course is free.The series is led by Assistant Director Meredith Perkins, who has six years of experience writing over 50 op-eds as a freelance journalist in student, local, and national publications. She won the 2024 and 2025 Region 4 Society of Professional Journalists Best College Opinion Writing award and the 2023 Ohio News Media Association Best Collegiate Column Writing award. A current Master of Public Affairs-Master of International Affairs student, her past newsroom experience inspires her to make complex academic conversations accessible for public audiences.Session 1: Before You Writewill introduce the history and purpose of op-eds and the range of places where opinion writing appears, including local and national newspapers, industry publications, departmental blogs, and platforms such as Substack. We will review genre conventions of op-eds, why op-eds are useful, and what information writers should know (e.g. workplace media policies) before considering publication.Session 2: Drafting Your First Op-Edwill focus on identifying a strong and timely argument. Participants will examine who is already writing about their topic, the dominant conversation surrounding it, and recent news or research that might create an opportunity for commentary. A central exercise will help participants identify the "knowledge gap" between what they know through expertise, research, or lived experience and what a general reader is likely to know. Participants will use that gap to develop a clear, relevant argument for a public audience.Session 3: Editing Your Op-Edwill help participants turn a draft into an accessible, publication-ready piece. Topics will include common word-count requirements, clear and concise language, reducing jargon, checking hyperlinks and sources, anticipating possible misunderstandings, proper image attribution, headline writing, and basic search engine optimization. After the session, participants can send drafts to the instructor for personalized feedback.Session 4: Publishing and Pitching Your Op-Edwill help participants identify the right outlet for their work based on the audience they hope to reach. The session will compare features and challenges of publishing in local and national newspapers, industry publications, institutional blogs, and independent platforms. Participants will learn what to include in a submission or pitch, such as a brief description, author bio, word count, contact information, and headshot, as well as how to recognize potential red flags. The session will conclude with an editor's perspective on what happens behind the inbox, including high submission volume, response times, competition for limited space, and why many submissions may be read without receiving a reply.By the end of the series, participants should understand how to identify a compelling op-ed idea, communicate specialized knowledge to a general audience, edit a piece to common publication standards, and develop a realistic strategy for publication. Participants who work on a piece throughout the program may leave with a completed or near-completed op-ed and a list of appropriate outlets to approach.       Register to attend at https://go.iu.edu/cVZV1S (https://go.iu.edu/cVZV1S) to get the Zoom link.

title: Treasures of the Silk Road
location: McCalla Center, McCalla Center, 525 E. 9th Street, Bloomington, IN 47408
description:
The McCalla Center, in collaboration with musician and scholar Shahyar Daneshgar, celebrates the opening of its new exhibition Treasures of the Silk Road on Friday, September 25th, 4:00 pm-6:00 pm EDT.
The exhibit features over 70 musical instruments from the Pastel-Daneshgar musical instrument collection, with a focus on strings, flutes, and percussion from across Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa. Crafted from wood, snakeskin, horsehair, lambskin, camel bone, and other unique materials, these instruments provide a compelling history of cultural and artistic exchanges that have led to the myriad musical sounds and styles that permeate the world today. The opening event will feature remarks from the collection owner, Shahyar Daneshgar, and will feature musical clips provided by the Lotus World Music & Arts Festival.
Shahyar Daneshgar is a lifelong musician, scholar, and cultural ambassador whose passion for traditional music has shaped more than three decades of collecting, teaching, and performing. Born into a large musical family, he studied at the Tehran Conservatory of Music before pursuing academic work in Germany and later at Indiana University, where he earned his Ph.D. in Central Eurasian Studies in 1995. He taught at Indiana University until his retirement in 2024. He is founder and director of the Bloomington Silk Road Ensemble.
The exhibition is free and runs from September 25, 2026, to September 2027.
The mission of the McCalla Center is to provide accessible exhibition and educational experiences, creating opportunities for students, faculty, and the community to engage with collections, IU-generated creative activity, and community projects in meaningful and innovative ways.

title: Igor Siddiqui | Contingent Communities lecture
location: Fine Arts Building, 1201 East 7th Street, Bloomington, IN 47405
description: Siddiqui's work—manifested as objects, images, texts, and events—links design experimentation to public engagement. He is interested in the role that interiors play in architectural experiments while advocating for experimentation in interiors as a distinct field of knowledge.Siddiqui's bookOblique Experiments: Claude Parent's Architectural Installations (1969–1975)is one of the first English-language monographs on French avant-garde architect Claude Parent and the first comprehensive study of his experimental interior installations from the 1970s. He recently editedInterior Experiments, a special triple-issue ofInteriors: Design/Architecture/Culture, where he has served as Editor-in-Chief, Co-Editor, and Associate Editor since 2016.His creative work has been exhibited at venues including the Tallinn Architecture Biennale, Contemporary Austin, SITE Santa Fe, and Fusebox Festival, and featured inDwell,Interior Design,Artforum, andTexas Architect. In 2022, Siddiqui received the IIDA Educator of the Year Award. He previously taught at the University of Pennsylvania, California College of the Arts, and Parsons. Siddiqui is a registered architect in Texas.Learn more at:https://www.igorsiddiqui.com@isssstudio on InstagramThe Eskenazi School's Comprehensive Design and Interior Design programs bring renowned designers to campus for public lectures and studio visits as part of the Design Speaker Series, generously supported with a gift from Reed Bobrick and Steve Tuchman.

title: Jazz @ the BCT: Natalie Boeyink Jazz Ensemble
location: Buskirk-Chumley Theatre, 114 E Kirkwood Ave, Bloomington, Indiana 47408
description:
About the Director
 Natalie Boeyink, bassist and educator, serves as associate professor of music jazz studies at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music. After earning her doctorate in music education at the Jacobs School in 2015, Boeyink spent eight years as a jazz lecturer and senior lecturer in the University of North Carolina system. She earned an M.M. in Jazz Performance at the University of Louisville and a B.M. in Jazz Studies at Jacobs. Her interest in the educational experiences and careers of jazzwomen has launched a series of research projects, conference presentations and publications, including her dissertation, “An Analysis and Description of Female Jazz Instrumentalists.” An advocate for jazzwomen, Boeyink served as chair of the Jazz Education Network’s Women in Jazz Committee and worked to reestablish the Sisters in Jazz Collegiate Combo Competition. Batuquê Trio is Boeyink’s seasoned collaboration with drummer Andy Smith and pianist Jamaal Baptiste. Focusing on contemporary Brazilian, Afro-Cuban, and Caribbean jazz, the trio frequently appears at jazz festivals as performers and clinicians. Their first CD, Transparency, was released in 2015. A second album is forthcoming in 2024. Some of Boeyink’s notable performances include appearances with Tammy McCann, Jamie Baum, Ingrid Jensen, Terri Lyne Carrington, Christine Jensen, Leni Stern, Jovino Santos Neto, Joe Piscopo, David “Fathead” Newman, Jon Hendricks, Jeff Coffin, David Liebman, and Lorraine Feather.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Osamu James Nakagawa: TRACE | Exhibition
location: FAR Center for Contemporary Arts, 202 S. Rogers St., Bloomington, IN 47404
description: Opening reception and artist talk: Friday, September 4, 58 pm  Nakagawa combines photographs taken at the sites of Japanese-American incarceration camps with photograms of found objects and rubbings of the memorials.  Using diptychs, Nakagawa pairs the past and the present, flattening the boundaries between them. TRACE seeks to reveal what can't be seen anymore, things that happened eighty years ago and have been quietly buried. Through a direct and immersive process, using actual objects and surfaces from the sites, Nakagawa unearths this history of forced incarceration.About the artist:  Osamu James Nakagawa was born in New York City in 1962, raised in Tokyo, and then returned to the US at the age of 15. He is the Distinguished Professor and the Ruth N. Halls Professor of Photography at Indiana University. Nakagawa is a recipient of the 2010 Guggenheim Fellowship, the 2010 Higashikawa New Photographer of the Year and 2015 Sagamihara Photographer of the Year in Japan.  Nakagawa's work has been exhibited internationally, selected solo exhibitions include PGI, Tokyo; Kyoto University of the Arts; Sepia EYE, New York; Sakima Art Museum, Okinawa, Japan; and others. Group shows include "A Shared Elegy" with Emmet Gowin and Elijah Gowin; and "After Photoshop" at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. His work is included in numerous public collections, including George Eastman Museum and the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum.  Link to the artist's website:https://jamesnakagawa.com/en (https://jamesnakagawa.com/en)  FAR Center for Contemporary Arts:https://thefar.org/events/event/121689 (https://thefar.org/events/event/121689)

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Excursions Into the Weird @ Cultural Arts Gallery
description: "ExcursionsIntothe Weird," is an exhibition of paintings by artist, author, and longtime Bradbury friend John CarterTibbetts, opening October 1 at the Cultural Arts Galleryat IUIndianapolis. title: Be a Part of the"Day in My Life"Series
Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.

description: Outfitting IU Athletics: Hoosier Champions                  This exhibit showcases objects from IU's championship teams and athletes, connecting them to historic achievements in the Big Ten and the national stage. When that organization closed, they donated their materials to IU. Steele, Indiana University's First Artist in ResidenceCapturing the Campus pays tribute to renowned Hoosier artist T.C. Steele. The exhibit honors the century that has passed since his death by showcasing paintings form the artist's residency at IU and other relevant works. The exhibit will bring together Steele's landscapes from the IU Public Art and Cultural Heritage Collection and the Indiana State Museum and Historic Sites' collection, allowing the holdings of these two collections to be viewed in one space. title: Treasures of the Silk Road
location: McCalla Center, McCalla Center, 525 E. 9th Street, Bloomington, IN 47408
description:
The McCalla Center, in collaboration with musician and scholar Shahyar Daneshgar, celebrates the opening of its new exhibition Treasures of the Silk Road on Friday, September 25th, 4:00 pm-6:00 pm EDT.
The exhibit features over 70 musical instruments from the Pastel-Daneshgar musical instrument collection, with a focus on strings, flutes, and percussion from across Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa. Crafted from wood, snakeskin, horsehair, lambskin, camel bone, and other unique materials, these instruments provide a compelling history of cultural and artistic exchanges that have led to the myriad musical sounds and styles that permeate the world today. The opening event will feature remarks from the collection owner, Shahyar Daneshgar, and will feature musical clips provided by the Lotus World Music & Arts Festival.
Shahyar Daneshgar is a lifelong musician, scholar, and cultural ambassador whose passion for traditional music has shaped more than three decades of collecting, teaching, and performing. Born into a large musical family, he studied at the Tehran Conservatory of Music before pursuing academic work in Germany and later at Indiana University, where he earned his Ph.D. in Central Eurasian Studies in 1995. He taught at Indiana University until his retirement in 2024. He is founder and director of the Bloomington Silk Road Ensemble.
The exhibition is free and runs from September 25, 2026, to September 2027.
The mission of the McCalla Center is to provide accessible exhibition and educational experiences, creating opportunities for students, faculty, and the community to engage with collections, IU-generated creative activity, and community projects in meaningful and innovative ways.

title: Fall 2026 CLACS Faculty Research Symposium with Luis A. González
description: CLACS Faculty Research Symposium welcomes Luis A. González, Librarian for Latin American, Spanish & Portuguese, Latino, and European Studies, and an Adjunct faculty in History at Indiana University as he presents: Books in Formerly Sacred Spaces: The Story of a Public Library, a President, and an Artist — Jiquilpan, Mexico, 1941   Abstract:  This presentation considers the Gabino Ortiz Public Library, notably founded by President Lázaro Cárdenas in his hometown of Jiquilpan, Michoacán, in 1941. As part of his national cultural project, President Cárdenas opened the library within a repurposed church which also houses murals by José Clemente Orozco depicting events from the Mexican Revolution. This case study presents a compelling opportunity to examine the intersections of state cultural policy, collective memory, and the social imaginary of the library in modern Mexico.   Biography:  Luis A. González is the Librarian for Latin American, Spanish & Portuguese, Latino, and European Studies, and an Adjunct faculty in History at Indiana University. He has published in the fields of Brazilian agrarian, social, and socio-legal history, and in Latin American Studies librarianship. Luis is a Contributing Editor for the Handbook of Latin American Studies, published by the Hispanic Division of the Library of Congress, and past president of the Seminar on the Acquisition of Latin American Library Materials (SALALM).

title: Chinese Tidings: "The Belt and Road Initiative: Domestic Policymaking and Global Impacts"
description: Pizza is served at 5:30 pm. and the lecture starts at 6:00 pm.About the lecture: Launched in 2013, the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) occupies a central position in China's contemporary foreign policy and domestic development  agenda. While often described as an infrastructure investment program, the BRI encompasses multiple dimensions of development policymaking, trade and investment facilitation, financial cooperation, and people-to-people exchange. Understanding how the initiative is organized and implemented is crucial for making sense of China's evolving position in the global economic and political system. This lecture provides a framework for understanding the BRI, with particular attention to its domestic organizing mechanisms, how they shape China's engagement with partner countries, and the broader implications of the initiative for global development.About the presenter: Dr. Hong Zhang is an Assistant Professor in the Department of International Studies at the Hamilton Lugar School. Her research focuses on the political economy of global development and China's role in it. She teaches courses on global development, infrastructure, and China–Global South relations. She is currently writing a book on China's developmental statecraft, examining how  China builds structural power in the global economy while strengthening its  developmental state at home.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Osamu James Nakagawa: TRACE | Exhibition
location: FAR Center for Contemporary Arts, 202 S. Rogers St., Bloomington, IN 47404
description: Opening reception and artist talk: Friday, September 4, 58 pm  Nakagawa combines photographs taken at the sites of Japanese-American incarceration camps with photograms of found objects and rubbings of the memorials.  Using diptychs, Nakagawa pairs the past and the present, flattening the boundaries between them. TRACE seeks to reveal what can't be seen anymore, things that happened eighty years ago and have been quietly buried. Through a direct and immersive process, using actual objects and surfaces from the sites, Nakagawa unearths this history of forced incarceration.About the artist:  Osamu James Nakagawa was born in New York City in 1962, raised in Tokyo, and then returned to the US at the age of 15. He is the Distinguished Professor and the Ruth N. Halls Professor of Photography at Indiana University. Nakagawa is a recipient of the 2010 Guggenheim Fellowship, the 2010 Higashikawa New Photographer of the Year and 2015 Sagamihara Photographer of the Year in Japan.  Nakagawa's work has been exhibited internationally, selected solo exhibitions include PGI, Tokyo; Kyoto University of the Arts; Sepia EYE, New York; Sakima Art Museum, Okinawa, Japan; and others. Group shows include "A Shared Elegy" with Emmet Gowin and Elijah Gowin; and "After Photoshop" at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. His work is included in numerous public collections, including George Eastman Museum and the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum.  Link to the artist's website:https://jamesnakagawa.com/en (https://jamesnakagawa.com/en)  FAR Center for Contemporary Arts:https://thefar.org/events/event/121689 (https://thefar.org/events/event/121689)

Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Excursions Into the Weird @ Cultural Arts Gallery
description: "ExcursionsIntothe Weird," is an exhibition of paintings by artist, author, and longtime Bradbury friend John CarterTibbetts, opening October 1 at the Cultural Arts Galleryat IUIndianapolis. title: Be a Part of the"Day in My Life"Series
Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

description: Outfitting IU Athletics: Hoosier Champions                  This exhibit showcases objects from IU's championship teams and athletes, connecting them to historic achievements in the Big Ten and the national stage. Founded in 1974 by the Culture and Ethnic Affairs Guild of the Oakland Museum of California, the Black Filmmakers Hall of Fame began as a film lecture series and awards ceremony celebrating achievements of Black film industry figures. When that organization closed, they donated their materials to IU. In collaboration with the IU Black Film Center and Archive, this exhibit features objects from that collection, including founding documents, costumes, and handprints of inductees to the Hall of Fame. Steele, Indiana University's First Artist in ResidenceCapturing the Campus pays tribute to renowned Hoosier artist T.C. Steele. The exhibit honors the century that has passed since his death by showcasing paintings form the artist's residency at IU and other relevant works. The exhibit will bring together Steele's landscapes from the IU Public Art and Cultural Heritage Collection and the Indiana State Museum and Historic Sites' collection, allowing the holdings of these two collections to be viewed in one space.        Dates: April 17, 2026 - April 2026                   Multipurpose Room          Currently Featuring: The Gift of Collecting: Tina Jernigan          Jernigan was a passionate supporter of both Indiana University and the arts. She donated artworks to the IU Public Art and Cultural Heritage Collection upon her passing in 2024. With funding provided by Jernigan, Public Art professionally framed, hung, and preserved these pieces for this exhibit in the McCalla Building and for future installations on campus.         Dates: July 2026-July 2027

title: Ostrom Workshop | Research Series: Diego Pacheco
location: The Ostrom Workshop, 513 N PARK AVE
description: Bio  Diego Pacheco Balanza is a Bolivian researcher, public policy specialist, and former diplomat with over two decades of experience in sustainable development, environmental governance, and international negotiations. He holds a Ph.D. in Public Policy from Indiana University, where he studied under Nobel Laureate Elinor Ostrom, an MSc in Rural Resources and Environmental Policy from Imperial College London, and a BA in Anthropology.  His work has focused on the relationships between society and Nature, institutional governance, Indigenous Peoples, climate change, biodiversity, and the development of the Living Well (Vivir Bien) approach and cosmobiocentric perspectives for sustainability. Most recently, he served as Director General for Living Well and Foreign Policy at the Office of the Vice President of the Plurinational State of Bolivia and as Chargé d'Affaires a.i. at the Permanent Mission of Bolivia to the United Nations in New York. He has also served twice as Bolivia's Vice Minister of Planning and represented the country in multilateral environmental negotiations under the UNFCCC, CBD, and IPBES. He is the author of numerous books and scientific publications on public policy, Mother Earth, natural resources governance and sustainable development. His current research explores new pathways for global governance through the integration of indigenous knowledge, collective action, and Mother Earth-centered approaches.Title  From Social–Ecological Systems toward Life Systems: Expanding Ostromian Institutional Analysis toward Mother Earth FuturesAbstract  Building on the growing recognition of Indigenous and local knowledge systems, plural worldviews, and relational approaches to human–Nature relationships, this talk explores how the Ostrom Workshop tradition of institutional analysis and collective action theory might be expanded to engage these non-anthropocentric perspectives. It considers a shift from an analytical focus on human actors as the primary agents of collective action within social–ecological systems toward Communities of Life within Life Systems, and introduces an analytical framework and empirical architecture for examining Human–Mother Earth co-flourishing. This also speaks to an emerging research gap concerning the joint examination of human and more-than-human outcomes, rather than treating their relationship predominantly in one direction.About the Ostrom Workshop Research Series  Learn about innovative research by Graduate Students and Visiting Scholars as they advance the mission of the Ostrom Workshop, building upon the theme of governance to understand and address major societal problems.
