The McCalla Center, in collaboration with musician and scholar Shahyar Daneshgar, celebrates the opening of its new exhibition Treasures of the Silk Road on Friday, September 25th, 4:00 pm-6:00 pm EDT.
The exhibit features over 70 musical instruments from the Pastel-Daneshgar musical instrument collection, with a focus on strings, flutes, and percussion from across Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa. Crafted from wood, snakeskin, horsehair, lambskin, camel bone, and other unique materials, these instruments provide a compelling history of cultural and artistic exchanges that have led to the myriad musical sounds and styles that permeate the world today. The opening event will feature remarks from the collection owner, Shahyar Daneshgar, and will feature musical clips provided by the Lotus World Music & Arts Festival.
Shahyar Daneshgar is a lifelong musician, scholar, and cultural ambassador whose passion for traditional music has shaped more than three decades of collecting, teaching, and performing. Born into a large musical family, he studied at the Tehran Conservatory of Music before pursuing academic work in Germany and later at Indiana University, where he earned his Ph.D. in Central Eurasian Studies in 1995. He taught at Indiana University until his retirement in 2024. He is founder and director of the Bloomington Silk Road Ensemble.
The exhibition is free and runs from September 25, 2026, to September 2027.
The mission of the McCalla Center is to provide accessible exhibition and educational experiences, creating opportunities for students, faculty, and the community to engage with collections, IU-generated creative activity, and community projects in meaningful and innovative ways.

title: Dedo Norris (fiddle), Jim Nelson (guitar), Sam Bartlett (banjo), Abby Ladin (bass), with calling by Tamara Loewenthal
Ballet Hispánico New York
description: Ballet Hispánico New York is the nation's leading American Latino dance company and the largest cultural institution of its kind in the United States. For over five decades, it has been a beacon of artistic excellence, celebrated for its bold repertory and exceptional training programs. The Bloomington performance will be an evening-length presentation of CARMEN.maquia. Since the debut in 1875, Carmen, the titular character from Bizet's opera, has become a timeless cultural icon, inspiring generations of composers, choreographers, and writers to attempt to capture her elusive and alluring nature. Ballet Hispánico honors the powerful Spanish leading lady with Gustavo Ramirez Sansano's electrifying CARMEN.maquia. One of today's most sought-after choreographers, Sansano's quintessential ballet invigorates this timeless tale with an unrelenting energy that leaves you breathless. Highly original and full of explosive movement, CARMEN.maquia is a bold reimagining of this tragic tale.

title: Émile Naoumoff, piano
description: Featuring the slow movements of Mozart's piano concertos K.453, K.467, K.491, K.271, and K.488About the ArtistÉmile Naoumoff is professor of music in piano at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music, where he has been on faculty since 1998. He has been likened to both Vladimir Horowitz and Arthur Rubinstein as a pianist, displaying, as one critic remarked, the fire of the former and the poetry of the latter. He revealed himself as a musical prodigy at age five, playing the piano and adding composition to his studies a year later. At age seven, he became the last disciple of Nadia Boulanger, who referred to him as "the gift of my old age." At age 18, he was signed by music publisher Schott, Mainz. Naoumoff studied with Boulanger until her death, permitting him also to work with Clifford Curzon, Igor Markevitch, and Robert and Gaby Casadesus, among others. Yehudi Menuhin conducted the premiere of Naoumoff's first piano concerto, with him as soloist, when Noumoff was 10 years old. Naoumoff pursued studies at the Paris Conservatory with Lelia Gousseau, Pierre Sancan, and Geneviève Joy, as well as at the École Normale de Musique de Paris with Pierre Dervaux (conducting). Upon Boulanger's death, he assumed her classes at the summer sessions of the Conservatoire d'Art Americain (Fontainebleau). He was later appointed to the Conservatoire National Supérieur de Musique, Paris. Naoumoff is regularly invited to perform by the world's premier orchestras, including the Los Angeles Philharmonic, Berlin Symphony, and Vienna Symphony, among many others. He has worked closely with such conductors as Leonard Bernstein, Leonard Slatkin, and Mstislav Rostropovich. He has also collaborated with a host of noteworthy musicians, including Jean-Pierre Rampal, Gerard Souzay, and Yo-Yo Ma. Naoumoff has been invited to perform at numerous music festivals, such as the Santander Summer Masterclasses, Verbier Academy Festival, Banff Center, and residencies at the Conservatory of Barcelona. He is an avid composer of French mélodies and is known for his transcriptions for the piano. He maintains a video journal of daily improvisations on his YouTube channel.
source: IU Jacobs School of Music, WFIU Community Calendar

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Osamu James Nakagawa: TRACE | Exhibition
location: FAR Center for Contemporary Arts, 202 S. Rogers St., Bloomington, IN 47404
description: Opening reception and artist talk: Friday, September 4, 58 pm  Nakagawa combines photographs taken at the sites of Japanese-American incarceration camps with photograms of found objects and rubbings of the memorials.  Using diptychs, Nakagawa pairs the past and the present, flattening the boundaries between them. TRACE seeks to reveal what can't be seen anymore, things that happened eighty years ago and have been quietly buried. Through a direct and immersive process, using actual objects and surfaces from the sites, Nakagawa unearths this history of forced incarceration.About the artist:  Osamu James Nakagawa was born in New York City in 1962, raised in Tokyo, and then returned to the US at the age of 15. He is the Distinguished Professor and the Ruth N. Halls Professor of Photography at Indiana University. Nakagawa is a recipient of the 2010 Guggenheim Fellowship, the 2010 Higashikawa New Photographer of the Year and 2015 Sagamihara Photographer of the Year in Japan.  Nakagawa's work has been exhibited internationally, selected solo exhibitions include PGI, Tokyo; Kyoto University of the Arts; Sepia EYE, New York; Sakima Art Museum, Okinawa, Japan; and others. Group shows include "A Shared Elegy" with Emmet Gowin and Elijah Gowin; and "After Photoshop" at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. His work is included in numerous public collections, including George Eastman Museum and the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum.  Link to the artist's website:https://jamesnakagawa.com/en (https://jamesnakagawa.com/en)  FAR Center for Contemporary Arts:https://thefar.org/events/event/121689 (https://thefar.org/events/event/121689)
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: Treasures of the Silk Road
location: McCalla Center, McCalla Center, 525 E. 9th Street, Bloomington, IN 47408
description:
The McCalla Center, in collaboration with musician and scholar Shahyar Daneshgar, celebrates the opening of its new exhibition Treasures of the Silk Road on Friday, September 25th, 4:00 pm-6:00 pm EDT.
The exhibit features over 70 musical instruments from the Pastel-Daneshgar musical instrument collection, with a focus on strings, flutes, and percussion from across Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa. Crafted from wood, snakeskin, horsehair, lambskin, camel bone, and other unique materials, these instruments provide a compelling history of cultural and artistic exchanges that have led to the myriad musical sounds and styles that permeate the world today. The opening event will feature remarks from the collection owner, Shahyar Daneshgar, and will feature musical clips provided by the Lotus World Music & Arts Festival.
Shahyar Daneshgar is a lifelong musician, scholar, and cultural ambassador whose passion for traditional music has shaped more than three decades of collecting, teaching, and performing. Born into a large musical family, he studied at the Tehran Conservatory of Music before pursuing academic work in Germany and later at Indiana University, where he earned his Ph.D. in Central Eurasian Studies in 1995. He taught at Indiana University until his retirement in 2024. He is founder and director of the Bloomington Silk Road Ensemble.
The exhibition is free and runs from September 25, 2026, to September 2027.
The mission of the McCalla Center is to provide accessible exhibition and educational experiences, creating opportunities for students, faculty, and the community to engage with collections, IU-generated creative activity, and community projects in meaningful and innovative ways.

location: Ford-Crawford Hall, Simon Music Center, 200 S. Eagleson Ave, Bloomington, Indiana 47405
description:
Five Friends Master Class Series – Honoring Robert Samels
 The Five Friends Master Class Series honoring the lives of five talented Jacobs School of Music students—Chris Carducci, Garth Eppley, Georgina Joshi, Zachary Novak, and Robert Samels—was established in 2012 with a gift of $1 million from the Georgina Joshi Foundation, Inc. This annual series of lectures, master classes, and residencies by a number of the world’s leading musicians and teachers focuses on areas of interest most relevant to the lives of the five friends—voice performance, choral conducting, early music, music theory, composition, and opera. The Georgina Joshi Foundation was established in 2007 as the vision of Georgina Joshi’s mother, Louise Addicott-Joshi, to provide educational and career development opportunities for young musicians and to encourage and support public performance of music. The gift to the school establishes a permanent way for the world to learn about each of the five friends, their musical talents and passions, and to encourage the development of similar talents and passions in current and future music students. The establishment of this endowment by the families is administered by the IU Foundation.
 Bass-baritone and composer Robert Samels was born on June 2, 1981, and died in a plane crash on April 20, 2006. He was a doctoral student in choral conducting at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music and had studied voice with Giorgio Tozzi and Costanza Cuccaro. He began his vocal studies with Alfred Anderson at the University of Akron and Andreas Poulimenos at Bowling Green State University. Samels had recently appeared as Mr. Gibbs in the world premiere of Our Town by Ned Rorem, as Marco in the collegiate premiere of William Bolcom’s A View from the Bridge, and as Joseph and Herod in the collegiate premiere of El Niño by John Adams. In September 2005, he conducted the premiere of his own opera, Pilatvs. As a member of the Wolf Trap Opera Company for 2006, he would have added three roles that summer, including Bartolo in Le Nozze di Figaro, Friar Laurence in Roméo et Juliette, and Pluto in Telemann’s Orpheus. Other opera credits included the title roles of Don Pasquale and Il Turco in Italia, as well as Leporello in Don Giovanni, Falstaff in The Merry Wives of Windsor, and Bottom in A Midsummer Night’s Dream. In the summer of 2004, he performed Creon in the New York premiere of John Eaton’s Antigone. Samels also frequently performed in the oratorio repertoire. In the spring of 2005, he was selected as a semi-finalist in the annual competition of the Oratorio Society of New York. He was an announcer with public radio station WFIU, as well as the host and producer of its Cantabile program. A soloist with Aguavá New Music Studio, he had recently performed a concert at the Library of Congress. Samels was an associate instructor in the Jacobs School’s Music Theory Department, where he was loved and admired by his students.

title: Guest Music Theory Lecture – Jonathan De Souza (Western University, Ontario), "Music Theory and Practice: A Violin-Based Analysis of 'Salut d'amour'"
description: Abstract  Music theory has traditionally focused on abstract musical structures and idealized listeners. Yet in recent years, the discipline has increasingly considered performance, embodiment, instruments, and related issues. So, current theory engages practice. How can we think about this apparent paradigm shift? And more generally, about the relation between music theory and practice? In this talk, I'll approach these questions while developing an analysis of Edward Elgar's Salut d'amour, op. 12, that draws on my experience as a theorist and a lifelong violinist. Ultimately, I'll argue that theory and practice, like mind and body, are fundamentally interconnected.Five Friends Master Class Series – Honoring Robert SamelsThe Five Friends Master Class Series honoring the lives of five talented Jacobs School of Music students—Chris Carducci, Garth Eppley, Georgina Joshi, Zachary Novak, and Robert Samelswas established in 2012 with a gift of $1 million from the Georgina Joshi Foundation, Inc. In the summer of 2004, he performed Creon in the New York premiere of John Eaton's Antigone. Samels also frequently performed in the oratorio repertoire. In the spring of 2005, he was selected as a semi-finalist in the annual competition of the Oratorio Society of New York. He was an announcer with public radio station WFIU, as well as the host and producer of its Cantabile program. A soloist with Aguavá New Music Studio, he had recently performed a concert at the Library of Congress. Samels was an associate instructor in the Jacobs School's Music Theory Department, where was loved and admired by his students.

description:
Powering the Alliance: Energy, Minerals, and the Race to Break China's Grip on Asia's Supply Chains
Dr. William Chou — Senior Fellow and Deputy Director, Japan Chair, Hudson Institute
China processes 90 percent of the world's rare earths and has twice cut off supply to Japan to win a political argument. It controls the inputs behind everything from electric vehicles to precision munitions. Dr. William Chou of the Hudson Institute explains how Beijing built that leverage, what it costs America and its allies, and what Washington and Tokyo are now spending hundreds of billions of dollars to undo. From Alaskan gas to rare earth magnets to the power plants behind the AI boom, this is the competition that will decide who sets the terms in the Indo-Pacific.
Hosted by the Alexander Hamilton Society at Indiana University. Free and open to the public.

title: AHS/21JPSI: "Powering the Alliance: Energy, Minerals, and the Race to Break China's Grip on Asia's Supply Chains" (Dr. William Chou, Hudson Institute)
description: This public event is open to all students, faculty, staff, and members of the community. Please join us!  ———————————–About the talk:In recent years, Beijing has used its control over rare earth processing and energy inputs to pressure Japan, the U.S. and other trading partners. This talk will examine what has happened and discuss how the US and Japan are jointly responding, including a $550 billion strategic investment fund, Alaska LNG, allied mineral processing, and a power buildout to support the AI and semiconductor race. This event is hosted by the student-run Alexander Hamilton Society and co-sponsored by 21JPSI.About the speaker: William Chou is a senior fellow and deputy director of Hudson Institute's Japan Chair. His work at Hudson focuses on the United States' relationship with Japan and other Indo-Pacific issues, especially economic security, trade and investment, and regional partnerships. Dr. Chou's recent projects include analyses of the Nippon Steel–US Steel partnership, economic security cooperation among the US, Japan, and the European Union, automotive and critical mineral supply chains, and US industrial and trade initiatives around the world.  Dr. Chou writes and speaks regularly on policy issues, with his analysis appearing in publications such as The Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg, Politico, The Washington Post, Nikkei, The New York Times, and the Financial Times.  He holds a BA in history from Yale and a PhD in history from the Ohio State University, with a dissertation and book manuscript on Cold War US-Japan commercial and diplomatic relations. He is a former fellow at the Smithsonian, the Clements Center at the University of Texas at Austin, and the University of Tokyo. He began his career as a research analyst at the Institute for Defense Analyses during the Iraq War.All 21JPSI events are 100% in-person unless otherwise noted. This event is hosted by the student-run IU chapter of the Alexander Hamilton Society. 21JPSI is pleased to co-sponsor.

description:
Union Board, in collaboration with IU's College of Arts and Sciences, welcomes Bill Nye for a moderated Q&A at IU Auditorium. Best known to generations of viewers as “Bill Nye the Science Guy,” Nye is an award-winning science educator, television presenter, mechanical engineer, author, and science advocate who has spent decades making science engaging and accessible to audiences of all ages. 
He created and hosted the Emmy Award-winning PBS series Bill Nye the Science Guy and has continued his work in science communication through television, books, documentaries, and public speaking. He currently serves as Chief Ambassador and Vice Chairman of the Board of The Planetary Society, where he advocates for space exploration and planetary science.
During this special evening, Nye will participate in a moderated conversation exploring science, curiosity, education, space exploration, and his remarkable career. This event offers an opportunity to hear from one of the world's most recognizable science communicators and explore the questions that inspire him, getting to know the science television star on a more personal level.

title: Matt Hightower, tuba
location: Ford-Crawford Hall, Simon Music Center, 200 S. Eagleson Ave, Bloomington, Indiana 47405
description:
Faculty Recital
 Repertoire and additional performers to be announced
 About the Artists
 Matt Hightower is assistant professor of music in tuba and euphonium at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music. Prior to his appointment at the Jacobs School, he held similar positions at the University of Kentucky (UK) and Texas A&M University-Kingsville. Hightower’s professional performance experience covers a wide range of chamber, orchestral, and solo music, spanning three continents and nine countries. He is a prizewinner of international solo competitions and has presented master classes to tuba/euphonium students around the world. His list of solo residencies include Baylor University, Conservatory of Reykjavik (Iceland), University of Louisiana at Monroe, University of Texas, the South Central Regional Tuba/Euphonium Conference, the South East Regional Tuba/Euphonium Conferences, The United States Army Band Tuba/Euphonium Workshop, and the Xi Xiang Music Valley (China), among others. He is tubist with the UK Faculty Brass Quintet and was previously tubist with the Corpus Christi and the Kingsville brass quintets. He is a founding member of the Atlas Tuba Quartet. Some of his credits as a large ensemble performer include appearances with the Bloomington Camerata Orchestra, Columbus (Indiana) Symphony, Evansville Philharmonic, Iceland Symphony Orchestra, Jackson Symphony, and David Baker’s 21st-Century Bebop Band. Hightower is also an award-winning composer. In 2010, he was named the winner of the KMEA Intercollegiate Composition Contest. Commissioned works by Hightower have received premier performances at the 2012, 2014, and 2016 International Tuba Conferences, the 2017 and 2018 South Central Regional Tuba Euphonium Conference, the 2018 South East Regional Tuba Euphonium Conference, the John F. Kennedy Center, and the 2016 Texas Music Educators Conference. Hightower earned a B.M. in Music Education from Murray State University, an M.M. in Tuba Performance from Jacobs, and a D.M.A. from the University of Texas at Austin. His primary instructors were Ray Conklin, Daniel Perantoni, and Charles Villarrubia, with additional instruction in the field of composition from Mike D’Ambrosio, John Fannin, and P.Q. Phan. Hightower is a B&S performing artist.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Osamu James Nakagawa: TRACE | Exhibition
location: FAR Center for Contemporary Arts, 202 S. Rogers St., Bloomington, IN 47404
description: Opening reception and artist talk: Friday, September 4, 58 pm  Nakagawa combines photographs taken at the sites of Japanese-American incarceration camps with photograms of found objects and rubbings of the memorials.  Using diptychs, Nakagawa pairs the past and the present, flattening the boundaries between them. TRACE seeks to reveal what can't be seen anymore, things that happened eighty years ago and have been quietly buried. Through a direct and immersive process, using actual objects and surfaces from the sites, Nakagawa unearths this history of forced incarceration.About the artist:  Osamu James Nakagawa was born in New York City in 1962, raised in Tokyo, and then returned to the US at the age of 15. He is the Distinguished Professor and the Ruth N. Halls Professor of Photography at Indiana University. Nakagawa is a recipient of the 2010 Guggenheim Fellowship, the 2010 Higashikawa New Photographer of the Year and 2015 Sagamihara Photographer of the Year in Japan.  Nakagawa's work has been exhibited internationally, selected solo exhibitions include PGI, Tokyo; Kyoto University of the Arts; Sepia EYE, New York; Sakima Art Museum, Okinawa, Japan; and others. Group shows include "A Shared Elegy" with Emmet Gowin and Elijah Gowin; and "After Photoshop" at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. His work is included in numerous public collections, including George Eastman Museum and the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum.  Link to the artist's website:https://jamesnakagawa.com/en (https://jamesnakagawa.com/en)  FAR Center for Contemporary Arts:https://thefar.org/events/event/121689 (https://thefar.org/events/event/121689)
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Be a Part of the"Day in My Life"Series
Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: Kelley Teaching Seminar-Analog Teaching to Promote Skill Mastery and Build Core Knowledge
location: WILLIAM J. GODFREY GRADUATE AND EXECUTIVE EDUCATION CENTER
description: The prevalence of electronic devices and artificial intelligence has unquestionably complicated the learning environment in today's college classroom. While instructors strive to communicate concepts, explain multiple-step processes, and invite students to participate in the co-creation of knowledge or practice demanding skills, students unfortunately often attend first to their devices for distraction or an easy answer.  The goal of the seminar will be to imagine how we can best help students master important skills and internalize the core business knowledge they will need as they navigate the ever-changing demands of the business world.  The seminar will include short presentations, ample discussion among colleagues, and demonstrations to illustrate some of the possibilities.

title: Global Competencies Skills Development Series: Multilateral Negotiations — Preparing to Get Consensus on a United Nations Resolution
description: What Is This? Can't stay the whole time, that is ok. This is a drop-in session.      No boring PowerPoint presentations. No passive lectures.As part of theGlobal Competencies Skills Development Series, this 2-hour interactive simulation drops you directly into a live humanitarian crisis scenario whereyoucall the shots. You'll work in interdisciplinary teams to navigate high-stakes international negotiations where conflicting political interests, limited resources, and rapid deadlines are on the line.  What You'll Get Out of It (Why You Need to Be Here)Day 1 Professional Tradecraft:Learn how diplomats and international crisis managers actually negotiate when peace talks stall or aid lines break.  Resume-Boosting Hard Skills:Gain hands-on practice inCritical Thinking, Strategic Communication, Crisis Leadership, and Teamwork—the top competencies global employers look for.  Direct Access to a Top Senior Executive:Work shoulder-to-shoulder with a veteran who managed over$4 Billionin international humanitarian aid and led UN refugee delegations.  Open to ALL staff, students, and faculty, and general public:Whether you're in HLS, O'Neill, Cybersecurity, Data Science, or Public Policy—undergrad or grad—these skills transfer directly to tech, government, intelligence, and international NGO careers.    Meet the Expert Paula Reed Lynchspent nearly five decades on the front lines of U.S. foreign policy and international relief. Serving 14 years in theSenior Executive Servicewithin the Department of State's Bureau of Population, Refugees, and Migration (PRM), Paula oversaw budgets exceeding$4 billionfor global disaster and refugee assistance.      The Highlights:    First American Rapporteur for the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).        Led interagency strategy across the Department of State and USAID.            Helped set global standards for international refugee protection across Africa and worldwide.            Recipient of the Secretary of State'sCareer Achievement Award.

title: Happiness 2.0 mask workshop
location: SIDNEY AND LOIS ESKENAZI MUSEUM OF ART
description: Throughout the fall semester, Indiana University undergraduate and high school students from the Bloomington community are invited to participate in the Happiness 2.0 Mask Workshops — an interactive experience that brings together science, art, and reflection on digital life.  The experience combines three components:an accessible discussion of current research on digital media and identity  a guided exploration of artworks in the Eskenazi Museum's galleries  a hands-on mask-making activity    Drawing inspiration from both the research discussion and the museum experience, participants will create a mask representing aspects of their own digital identity and experiences with digital media. Topics explored throughout the workshop include identity formation, online self-presentation, the relationship between online and offline selves, and well-being.

title: CLACS Global Health Series Workshop with Charlotte Scott: Introduction to Implementation Research in a Global Health Setting
description: CLACS Global Health Workshop with Charlotte Scott (https://fairbanks.indianapolis.iu.edu/about/directory/scott-charlotte.html), MSc  Lecturer, Community and Global HealthSchool of Public Health, Indiana University Indianapolis  How do we move effective public health interventions from research into real-world practice and make sure they work within the communities they are intended to serve?  Join the Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies (CLACS) for a Global Health Series Workshop with Charlotte Scott, MSc, Lecturer in Community and Global Health at the IU Richard M. Fairbanks School of Public Health.Implementation research is a field that is still growing, but it is a key contributor to effective global health programs and policies, as well as individual practices. Implementation research identifies and investigates problems that prevent effective implementation of interventions, develops and tests implementation strategies that provide solutions to these implementation problems, and obtains information to guide scale-up and sustainability. Its focus is on real-world conditions, aiming to work with the intended population, in the specific context, and under the actual influential factors. This workshop will offer an introduction to the topic and an opportunity to reflect on these concepts with a real-world example.   Scott brings extensive experience working in Colombia. Before joining IU, she worked with the International Center for Medical Training and Research (CIDEIM) and the Social Innovation in Health Initiative (SIHI) in Cali, Colombia contributing to community-based health research and public health training.   About the CLACS Global Health Series  The CLACS Global Health Series brings together students, faculty, practitioners, and community members to explore health challenges and public health initiatives across Latin America and the Caribbean. Developed in coordination with Whitney Cordoba-Grueso, MD, PhD, MPH, the series connects regional knowledge with interdisciplinary perspectives on global health, including mental and reproductive health, infectious and chronic disease, migration, environmental health, and health equity.This event is free and open to everyone. Students, faculty, staff, and members of the wider community are welcome.Planning to attend?  Please register using the button below. Registration is requested to assist organizers with planning.
source: IU Hamilton Lugar School, IU La Casa Latino Cultural Center

title: Social Structures and Developments within the Early Zoroastrian Community as Reflected in the Avesta
description: The Avesta is a valuable historical source for reconstructing the social organization of the early Zoroastrian community. The sacred and ritual character of the text predetermined the use of stable formulas and the creation of an ideal model of society. Nevertheless, behind this standardized framework, one can reconstruct mechanisms of intra‑communal regulation, power, and status relations.  This talk offers a systemic view of the social structure of the early Zoroastrian community, drawing on an analysis of the social terminology and the content of the Avesta. The presence of chronological layers within the Avesta allows us to trace the gradual increase in complexity of social institutions, as well as the evolution of interpersonal relations and power structures in the Zoroastrian community. These changes reflect the transition from small tribal collectives to more complex pre‑state formations. Thus, the Avesta recorded not so much a static model of society as the dynamics of development and adaptation of its social institutions.This event will take place on Zoom only.This event is sponsored by:Department of Central Eurasian Studies (CEUS)Inner Asian and Uralic National Resource Center (IAUNRC)

title: Who are Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders? (WAAPI) A Lunch Discussion On "[GI5.1][GI5.2]The Mamdani Effect & The Midterms"
location: Asian Culture Center (807 E 10th street, Bloomington, IN)
description: How do global political labels impact our national/local communities during election season, and vice versa? This month, WAAPI explores the "Mamdani effect", a particular case of how the political categorization of cultural and religious identities shapes public perception. We'll discuss "representation": while Mamdani gives important visibility to South Asian and Muslim voices, that same spotlight has unfortunately led to a rise in Islamophobia and anti-Asian hate. We will also look at "expectations": while many South Asians are known for working in tech, business, or medicine, Mamdani breaks that mold as a youthful politician. Join us for an open, student-led conversation. Free lunch is provided, and all students are welcome!  WAAPI is a monthly roundtable discussion by and for students interested in learning and discussing issues impacting the Asian American and Pacific Islander (AAPIs) and the general community. title: Byrnes Institute Colloquium: Madeline Stull, "Makeshift Modernity: The (In)Formal Urbanization of Interwar Belgrade"
description: This talk examines the (in)formal dynamics of Belgrade's urbanization during the interwar period, focusing on the parallel development of residential and municipal infrastructure in two adjacent neighborhoods: Jatagan-mala, the city's largest informal settlement, and Kotež Neimar, a privately developed neighborhood. Challenging narratives that marginalize the urban poor as peripheral to the city's development, Stull argues that informal settlement and formal planning were mutually constitutive processes. Drawing on archival documents, urban plans, and contemporary reporting, she shows how a regulatory and property-centered modernizing logic structured Belgrade's growth through displacement and dispossession. Municipal anxieties about the city's form and order materialized in the streets, producing hierarchies of urban belonging and practices of ownership grounded in bourgeois respectability, with violent consequences for the city's majority-poor population.  Madeline Stull is a Ph.D. candidate in East European History (with minors in Cultural History and Digital Humanities) at Indiana University, Bloomington. She earned a Master's and Bachelor of Arts in European History from Arizona State University and Barrett, the Honor's College in 2020 and 2021 respectively. Her research has been supported by the U.S. Fulbright Commission and an American Councils research fellowship. Madeline's most recent publication, "The Fantasy of Reason: Reevaluating Belgrade's 20th Century Urban Plans through Borislav Pekić's Houses," is available in Historical Geography issue no. 52. She is currently working on a dissertation entitled, Makeshift Modernity: The Creation of Belgrade at the Intersection of (In)Formality, which historizes and spatializes the marginalization of Belgrade's urban Others to better understand the genealogy of modern urban management practices in a newly formed, peripheral nation.

title: Treasures of the Silk Road
location: McCalla Center, McCalla Center, 525 E. 9th Street, Bloomington, IN 47408
description:
The McCalla Center, in collaboration with musician and scholar Shahyar Daneshgar, celebrates the opening of its new exhibition Treasures of the Silk Road on Friday, September 25th, 4:00 pm-6:00 pm EDT.
The exhibit features over 70 musical instruments from the Pastel-Daneshgar musical instrument collection, with a focus on strings, flutes, and percussion from across Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa. Crafted from wood, snakeskin, horsehair, lambskin, camel bone, and other unique materials, these instruments provide a compelling history of cultural and artistic exchanges that have led to the myriad musical sounds and styles that permeate the world today. The opening event will feature remarks from the collection owner, Shahyar Daneshgar, and will feature musical clips provided by the Lotus World Music & Arts Festival.
Shahyar Daneshgar is a lifelong musician, scholar, and cultural ambassador whose passion for traditional music has shaped more than three decades of collecting, teaching, and performing. Born into a large musical family, he studied at the Tehran Conservatory of Music before pursuing academic work in Germany and later at Indiana University, where he earned his Ph.D. in Central Eurasian Studies in 1995. He taught at Indiana University until his retirement in 2024. He is founder and director of the Bloomington Silk Road Ensemble.
The exhibition is free and runs from September 25, 2026, to September 2027.
The mission of the McCalla Center is to provide accessible exhibition and educational experiences, creating opportunities for students, faculty, and the community to engage with collections, IU-generated creative activity, and community projects in meaningful and innovative ways.

title: Partita: An Evening with Barbara Kingsolver
location: IU Auditorium, 1211 E. 7th Street, Bloomington, IN 47405
description:
Join Pulitzer Prize-winning author Barbara Kingsolver for an evening of readings, questions, and musical performances by Jacobs School of Music pianist Susan Tsai to celebrate the release of her brand-new novel Partita.
Barbara Kingsolver is the author of ten bestselling works of fiction, including the novels Unsheltered, The Bean Trees, and The Poisonwood Bible, as well as books of poetry, essays, creative nonfiction, and Coyote’s Wild Home, a children’s book co-authored with Lily Kingsolver. She also collaborated with family members on the influential Animal, Vegetable, Miracle: A Year of Food Life. Kingsolver’s work has been translated into more than thirty languages and has earned a devoted readership at home and abroad. She is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Letters, and has received numerous awards and honors including the 2023 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction for her novel, Demon Copperhead, the National Humanities Medal, and most recently, the National Book Foundation's Medal for Distinguished Contribution to American Letters. She lives with her husband on a farm in southern Appalachia.
Partita is a deeply moving, unforgettable novel about art, music, class, memory, and the life-altering power of love—a book she says she has been waiting her whole life to write. Livia Cable has made her peace with her marriage and modest livelihood in the farm country where she grew up, until a shocking phone call from an old lover shakes her to the core. Decades earlier, this man knew her as Livia Bohusz, a music conservatory student estranged from her home and family, uncertain of anything except her passion for music and her promise as an extraordinary pianist. His request, now, to see her again stirs up ghosts she has kept at bay for a lifetime.
Shifting between past and present, Livia’s decision to meet or reject the reunion means confronting, step by step, in memories framed as musical dances, the experiences of childhood loss, abandonment, self-immolating passion, and perilous attachment to a man who broke her belief in love and ruptured the course of her life.
With razor-sharp acuity, Kingsolver’s new novel reflects on class barriers, the risks of ambition, and the timeless, life-changing powers of art. Told in movements that mirror a Bach partita, the novel unfolds with the precision and emotional power of music itself: each section building on the last, each theme returning transformed.

He presented the first TED talk on the topic of tuba and is one of the most popular classical musicians on YouTube with more than eight million views. His multifaceted musical career as a soloist and recording artist has taken him all over the world. He regularly gives master classes and clinics at major universities worldwide. Since 2022, he has served as professor of tuba at the Norwegian Academy of Music. His engagements include performances with such orchestras as the Oslo Philharmonic Orchestra, Warsaw Philharmonic Orchestra, the Taipei National Symphony Orchestra and Singapore Philharmonic. Baadsvik has performed in some of the most famous venues in the world, and 2006 marked his New York recital debut at Carnegie Hall. Baadsvik is an active recording artist whose CDs receive unstinting praise. In their review of Tuba Works, American Record Guide remarked, "This spectacular recording establishes Baadsvik as one of the best solo tubists in the world." Film composer John Williams said about Baadsvik's recording of his tuba concerto: "His rendering of my concerto far surpasses anything a composer might hope for." Visit baadsvik.com for audio clips and further information.Tomoko Kashiwagi is visiting lecturer in the Chamber and Collaborative Music Department at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music for the 2026-27 school year. Kashiwagi is associate professor of piano and collaborative piano and holds the Emily J. McAllister Endowed Chair at the University of Arkansas, where she joined the faculty in 2012. She is also the founder of the Ozark Music Initiative, a nonprofit dedicated to building community through music. Her work has been supported by multiple Mid-America Arts Alliance grants. In 2025, she was inducted into the Steinway & Sons Music Teacher Hall of Fame in recognition of her commitment and passion as piano educator. She has presented multiple times at CollabFest, the conference of the International Keyboard Collaborative Arts Society. She maintains an active performance career across the United States and internationally, exploring a wide range of repertoire. She earned a Bachelor of Music, Master of Music, and Performer Diploma in Piano Performance from the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music studying with renowned pianist Shigeo Neriki. Kashiwagi later became the first recipient of the Doctor of Musical Arts in Collaborative Piano degree from the University of Texas at Austin, where she studied with Anne Epperson.

title: Chamber Orchestra – Thomas Wilkins, conductor; Stephen Wyrczynski, viola soloist
description: Enjoy this performance from almost anywhere in the world viaLIVE@jacobs!Repertoire  Milhaud: La création du monde, Op. 81a (1923)Martin: Ballade for viola and wind orchestra (1972)Chadwick: Symphony No. 3 in F Major (1894)About the ArtistsThomas Wilkins is principal conductor of the Hollywood Bowl Orchestra, artistic partner for education and external engagement and Germeshausen Family and Youth Concerts Conductor Chair with the Boston Symphony Orchestra, and professor of music (conducting) at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music, where he holds the Henry A. Upper Chair of Orchestral Conducting, established by the late Barbara and David Jacobs as a part of Indiana University's Matching the Promise Campaign. He is also music director laureate of the Omaha Symphony, where he was music director from 2005 through 2021, and principal guest conductor of the Virginia Symphony Orchestra. Past positions have included resident conductor of the Detroit Symphony and the Florida Orchestra (Tampa Bay) and associate conductor of the Richmond (Virginia) Symphony. He also has served on the music faculties of North Park University (Chicago), University of Tennessee in Chattanooga, and Virginia Commonwealth University in Richmond. Devoted to promoting a life-long enthusiasm for music, Wilkins brings energy and commitment to audiences of all ages. He is hailed as a master at communicating and connecting with audiences. He has guest conducted orchestras throughout the United States. Wilkins' commitment to community has been demonstrated by his participation on several boards of directors, including the Greater Omaha Chamber of Commerce, the Charles Drew Health Center (Omaha), the Center Against Spouse Abuse in Tampa Bay, and the Museum of Fine Arts as well as the Academy Preparatory Center both in St. Petersburg, Florida. Currently, he serves as chairman of the board for the Raymond James Charitable Endowment Fund and as National Ambassador for the non-profit World Pediatric Project, headquartered in Richmond, Virginia, which provides children throughout Central America and the Caribbean with critical surgical and diagnostic care. A native of Norfolk, Virginia, Wilkins is a graduate of the Shenandoah Conservatory of Music and the New England Conservatory of Music (Boston). He and his wife, Sheri-Lee, are the proud parents of twin daughters, Erica and Nicole.Stephen Wyrczynski is currently professor of music in viola at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music. He was a member of the Philadelphia Orchestra for 18 years, joining them in 1992. Wyrczynski regularly performs as a soloist and chamber musician. He prioritizes faculty-student collaborations. One such partnership, which he cofounded with the late violinist Jorja Fleezanis, was an exploration of music from the Second Viennese School, in which faculty and students together performed music by Schoenberg, Webern, and Berg. Wyrczynski considers his teaching a direct result of his own relationship to performing, practicing, and listening. Teaching a student about the great privilege it is to serve the composers of our repertoire is one of the best ways for the students to gain ownership of their musical training. Most recently, he has completed a transcription of Igor Stravinsky's Rite of Spring with pianist Aram Arakelyan. Wyrczynski and Arakelyan gave the world premiere in the fall of 2024 and recorded it for Azica Records in the summer of 2025 with producer Alan Bise. A printed edition is published by Songburd Music. Wyrczynski will join the faculty of the Shepherd School of Music at Rice University in 2027.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Osamu James Nakagawa: TRACE | Exhibition
location: FAR Center for Contemporary Arts, 202 S. Rogers St., Bloomington, IN 47404
description: Opening reception and artist talk: Friday, September 4, 58 pm  Nakagawa combines photographs taken at the sites of Japanese-American incarceration camps with photograms of found objects and rubbings of the memorials.  Using diptychs, Nakagawa pairs the past and the present, flattening the boundaries between them. TRACE seeks to reveal what can't be seen anymore, things that happened eighty years ago and have been quietly buried. Through a direct and immersive process, using actual objects and surfaces from the sites, Nakagawa unearths this history of forced incarceration.About the artist:  Osamu James Nakagawa was born in New York City in 1962, raised in Tokyo, and then returned to the US at the age of 15. He is the Distinguished Professor and the Ruth N. Halls Professor of Photography at Indiana University. Nakagawa is a recipient of the 2010 Guggenheim Fellowship, the 2010 Higashikawa New Photographer of the Year and 2015 Sagamihara Photographer of the Year in Japan.  Nakagawa's work has been exhibited internationally, selected solo exhibitions include PGI, Tokyo; Kyoto University of the Arts; Sepia EYE, New York; Sakima Art Museum, Okinawa, Japan; and others. Group shows include "A Shared Elegy" with Emmet Gowin and Elijah Gowin; and "After Photoshop" at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. His work is included in numerous public collections, including George Eastman Museum and the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum.  Link to the artist's website:https://jamesnakagawa.com/en (https://jamesnakagawa.com/en)  FAR Center for Contemporary Arts:https://thefar.org/events/event/121689 (https://thefar.org/events/event/121689)

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Be a Part of the"Day in My Life"Series
Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.

title: Dinara Klinton, piano
description: RepertoireChopin: Twelve Etudes, Op. 10 (1830-32)Chopin: Trois nouvelles études, B.130 (1839)Chopin: Twelve Etudes, Op. 25 (1835-37)About the Artist  Ukrainian pianist Dinara Klinton is associate professor of music in piano at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music. After winning prizes in such international competitions as Busoni, Cleveland, BNDS, and Paderewski, she embarked on a busy international concert schedule, appearing at festivals including the Progetto Martha Argerich in Lugano, Cheltenham Music Festival, Aldeburgh Proms, and La Roque d'Antheron. Klinton has performed at many of the world's major concert venues, including the Royal Albert Hall, Royal Festival Hall, Barbican Centre, and Wigmore Hall in London, Berliner Philharmonie, Laeiszhalle and Elbphilharmonie Hamburg, Gewandhaus Leipzig, New York 92Y, Cleveland Severance Hall, Tokyo Sumida Triphony Hall, Great Hall of Moscow Conservatory, and Tchaikovsky Concert Hall. Her concerto engagements include orchestras such as the Philharmonia, Royal Philharmonic, Lucerne Symphony, Richmond Symphony, and Elgin Symphony. Klinton is also a dedicated educator and has combined her performance career with faculty positions at the Royal College of Music and the Yehudi Menuhin School. As a recording artist, she has received widespread critical acclaim. Her album Franz Liszt's Études d'exécution transcendante, released by the German label GENUIN Classics, received glowing reviews and was selected by BBC Music Magazine as Recording of the Month. She recorded her debut album, Music of Chopin and Liszt, at age 16 with American label Delos. Other albums include Chopin's music by the Fryderyk Chopin Institute in Poland, Prokofiev Complete Piano Sonatas, released by Piano Classics, and Mily Balakirev: Piano Concerto No. 1 on Dabringhaus und Grimm. Klinton's music education began at age five in her native Kharkiv, Ukraine. She graduated with highest honors from the Moscow Central Music School under Valery Piassetski and the Moscow State Conservatory P. I. Tchaikovsky under Eliso Virsaladze. She then earned a master's degree and artist diploma from the Royal College of Music in London under Dina Parakhina. She also studied with William Grant Nabore, Stanislav Ioudenitch, and Dang Thai Son, among others, at the Lake Como Piano Academy and worked with Boris Petrushansky at the Imola Piano Academy.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Osamu James Nakagawa: TRACE | Exhibition
location: FAR Center for Contemporary Arts, 202 S. Rogers St., Bloomington, IN 47404
description: Opening reception and artist talk: Friday, September 4, 58 pm  Nakagawa combines photographs taken at the sites of Japanese-American incarceration camps with photograms of found objects and rubbings of the memorials.  Using diptychs, Nakagawa pairs the past and the present, flattening the boundaries between them. TRACE seeks to reveal what can't be seen anymore, things that happened eighty years ago and have been quietly buried. Through a direct and immersive process, using actual objects and surfaces from the sites, Nakagawa unearths this history of forced incarceration.About the artist:  Osamu James Nakagawa was born in New York City in 1962, raised in Tokyo, and then returned to the US at the age of 15. He is the Distinguished Professor and the Ruth N. Halls Professor of Photography at Indiana University. Nakagawa is a recipient of the 2010 Guggenheim Fellowship, the 2010 Higashikawa New Photographer of the Year and 2015 Sagamihara Photographer of the Year in Japan.  Nakagawa's work has been exhibited internationally, selected solo exhibitions include PGI, Tokyo; Kyoto University of the Arts; Sepia EYE, New York; Sakima Art Museum, Okinawa, Japan; and others. Group shows include "A Shared Elegy" with Emmet Gowin and Elijah Gowin; and "After Photoshop" at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. His work is included in numerous public collections, including George Eastman Museum and the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum.  Link to the artist's website:https://jamesnakagawa.com/en (https://jamesnakagawa.com/en)  FAR Center for Contemporary Arts:https://thefar.org/events/event/121689 (https://thefar.org/events/event/121689)
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design
