title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Frances Lightbound: The Land Dissolves in Water | Exhibition
description: Lecture: October 27, 6:30–8pmExhibition: October 27–December 6, 2026, Mon.–Thur. 10am–4pm when IU classes are in session  Lightbound studies the production of space in urban environments, weaving narratives across photography, print, spatial interventions, and sculpture, with a focus on materials and sites in transition.  Architecture becomes an entry-point to questions of land use, ownership and access, bodily experience and perception, and timeframes ranging from the human to the geological. Lightbound invites viewers to consider and participate in the continual (re)construction of meaning in urban environments.  Frances Lightbound holds a B.A. from Glasgow School of Art, Scotland, and an M.F.A. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Recent solo exhibitions include Louise Hopkins Center for the Arts (Lubbock, TX), RULE Gallery (Marfa, TX), and the John David Mooney Foundation (Chicago, IL); her work has been exhibited internationally at venues in London, Glasgow and Berlin. Lightbound is a Lecturer at School of the Art Institute of Chicago in the departments of Print media and Photography.The J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program Lecture and Exhibition Series brings prominent working artists and architects to Columbus. Lectures take place in the auditorium and exhibitions in the gallery, both located within The Republic Building, 333 Second Street in Columbus. The gallery is open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. All events are free and open to the public.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: HIV/STI Testing
description: Free HIV Testing & Safer Sex Supplies at the LGBTQ+ Culture Center  Taking care of your sexual health is an important part of your overall well-being, and we're committed to making resources accessible, welcoming, and judgment-free.Positive Link (https://iuhealth.org/find-medical-services/positive-link-hiv-services) provides free and confidential HIV testing in Room 204 of the LGBTQ+ Culture Center every Thursday from 10:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. during the academic year. During the summer, testing is available on the first and third Thursdays of each month.  In addition, during the academic year, the Monroe County Health Department offers free chlamydia and gonorrhea testing on the third Thursday of every month, also from 10:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. in Room 101.  The LGBTQ+ Culture Center also offers a variety of free safer sex supplies, including condoms, internal condoms, dental dams, lubricants, and educational materials on proper use. These resources are available to all students, free of charge. You can find them in the kitchenette area near the back entrance of the Center and are welcome to take what you need.  STI Testing & Safer Sex Resources Beyond Campus  Prioritizing your sexual health should be simple and accessible. In addition to services available at the LGBTQ+ Culture Center, students can receive testing on campus through the IU Student Health Center (https://healthcenter.indiana.edu/medical/sti-testing/index.html) or visit several local organizations (https://healthcenter.indiana.edu/health-answers/sexual-health/sti-testing-resources.html) that offer free or low-cost testing and prevention services.  Many of these providers offer confidential care, safer sex supplies, and supportive information about prevention, treatment, and sexual wellness. If you're unsure where to start, we're happy to help connect you with resources that fit your needs.All Indiana University events, groups, activities, educational, cultural, and historical observances welcome all members of the Indiana University community.

description: Outfitting IU Athletics: Hoosier Champions                  This exhibit showcases objects from IU's championship teams and athletes, connecting them to historic achievements in the Big Ten and the national stage. Founded in 1974 by the Culture and Ethnic Affairs Guild of the Oakland Museum of California, the Black Filmmakers Hall of Fame began as a film lecture series and awards ceremony celebrating achievements of Black film industry figures. When that organization closed, they donated their materials to IU. In collaboration with the IU Black Film Center and Archive, this exhibit features objects from that collection, including founding documents, costumes, and handprints of inductees to the Hall of Fame. Steele, Indiana University's First Artist in ResidenceCapturing the Campus pays tribute to renowned Hoosier artist T.C. Steele. The exhibit will bring together Steele's landscapes from the IU Public Art and Cultural Heritage Collection and the Indiana State Museum and Historic Sites' collection, allowing the holdings of these two collections to be viewed in one space. title: Global Competencies Skills Development Series: Mapping a Refugee Camp — Interactive Policy Simulation with Ambassador Gina Abercrombie-Winstanley
description: Real Crisis. Real Decisions. Real Tradecraft.  When displacement crises hit, how do international leaders manage logistics, security, human rights, and geopolitical pressure in real time?  Skip the standard lecture and get your hands on actual diplomatic decision-making. Join the Global Competencies Skills Development Series for Mapping a Refugee Camp, an interactive, fast-paced crisis response simulation led by Ambassador Gina Abercrombie-Winstanley—former U.S. Ambassador to Malta, 30-year Foreign Service veteran, and President of the Middle East Policy Council.  Having led emergency war-zone evacuations and served across Baghdad, Cairo, and Jeddah, Ambassador Abercrombie-Winstanley will guide you through the complex tradecraft, resource constraints, and tactical choices required on the front lines of global humanitarian crisis management.  Who Can Attend? Open to all: Students (Undergrad & Grad), Faculty, Staff, and the Public. (Light snacks and drinks provided)     What You'll Get Out of It      Hands-On Tactical Experience: Practice real-world decision-making under competing geopolitical, logistical, and ethical pressures.          Direct Professional Access: Work through crisis scenarios directly alongside a senior diplomat who operated across the State Department, Defense Department, and National Security Council.          Resume-Building Tradecraft: Build core skills in crisis navigation, strategic negotiation, and rapid resource allocation—essential for careers in foreign policy, intelligence, NGOs, and national security.          Active Networking: Team up with peers, faculty, and practitioners across campus over light refreshments.      Bio: Ambassador Gina Abercrombie-Winstanley  Ambassador Gina Abercrombie-Winstanley is a 30-year diplomat, former U.S. Ambassador to the Republic of Malta, and President of the Middle East Policy Council. Her career spans executive leadership roles across the Department of State, Defense Department, National Security Council, and Senate Foreign Relations Committee. She has advised the commander of U.S. cyber forces, expanded international counterterrorism partnerships, and led the emergency evacuation of thousands of U.S. citizens from a war zone. She is a recipient of the State Department Superior Honor Award for acts of courage during an al-Qaeda attack on the U.S. Consulate in Jeddah.

description: Xiao Hai was born in Shangqiu City in Henan Province in China. His debut book-length translation, Adrift in the South, a memoir by Xiao Hai, was published by Granta Magazine Editions in May, 2026.  His short-form translations have appeared in Granta, The Wall Street Journal, The Georgia Review, The Offing, Books from Taiwan, Florescence (The Taipei Chinese PEN), MAYDAY Magazine, and elsewhere. description: When Xiao Hai turned fifteen, his family paid a vocational-school teacher 1,200 yuan to find him a factory job in Shenzhen. So began fifteen years spent moving between the garment mills and electronics factories of China's fast-growing southern cities.Adrift in the South is a memoir of life as a migrant labourer in the twenty-first century, making iPhones and baby clothes, hand-stitching football shirts and cutting plastic into radios. Here, Xiao Hai reveals the alienation and tedium of factory life, the small indignities and indifference of the larger system. And he tells the story of how poetry led him somewhere unexpected: to join a small community of artists living, working, and studying together on the outskirts of Beijing.  This memoiris a landmark text from China's migrant worker literature movement, a grassroots group of writers providing an unvarnished account of what life is like for the 300 million migrant workers powering the world's second-biggest economy.About the author: Xiao Hai was born in Shangqiu City in Henan Province in China. At fifteen he moved to Shenzhen to join the workforce, moving between cities and factory jobs while writing poetry in his spare time. He is the author of the poetry collection Sisyphus on the Wenyu River, and translations of his poetry have appeared in World Literature Today and Chinese Literature Today.About the translator: Tony Hao is a New Haven, Connecticut-based Chinese-to-English literary translator and writer. Authors he has translated include Taiwanese novelist Tong Wei-Ger 童偉格, Chinese worker-poet Xiao Hai 小海, Taiwanese transgender writer Liu Chen-Chun 劉宸君, and Chinese short story writer Ban Yu 班宇.  His debut book-length translation, Adrift in the South, a memoir by Xiao Hai, was published by Granta Magazine Editions in May, 2026. title: Uncovering Our Past: Public Archaeology Day, Salt Creek SRA (Monroe Lake)
location: Monroe Lake, Salt Creek State Recreation Area, southern/eastern end of Monroe Dam Road (ignore State Road 446 address)
description:
Public Archaeology Day from 1 to 4 p.m.
Monroe Lake: Salt Creek SRA

Before Monroe Lake was built, the Salt Creek Valley was home to numerous small family farms, some dating back to the 1820s. While most homesteads have been reclaimed by time and nature, remnants remain in the form of scattered foundation stones, piles of rock and brick from collapsed chimneys, wells and cisterns, and fragments of metal and pottery.

Archaeologists from the Indiana Division of Historic Preservation and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Louisville District are partnering with the Indiana Division of State Parks to document some of these historic sites. Members of the public can assist with mapping sites and conducting shovel probes to search for artifacts or just stop by to view the work and ask questions. 

If you would like to assist the archaeologists, advance registration is encouraged by noon on Nov. 4 – but walk-up volunteers are also welcome!

Salt Creek SRA is located at the eastern/southern end of Monroe Dam Road in Bloomington (the eastern end of the Monroe Lake reservoir dam); entrance is free. When you arrive, look for signs directing you to the archaeological work site. Please note that the work site is not accessible; it is located in the woods and may require walking up to 1/3-mile on uneven ground.

title: Scholarly Write-In
description:

We will check in at the beginning of our meeting, set some goals together, then work independently for a few hours. Fifteen minutes prior to the close of the meeting, we will reconvene to update each other on our progress and set broad goals for the coming week.

This is a casual meeting – feel free to come for as much or as little time as you like, and only during the weeks that work for you. You are welcome and encouraged to work on anything that you need time and space for: participants regularly work on dissertations, course papers, syllabi and lesson plans, articles and pieces for publication, and grading. Our goal is to create a space where we can work together in solidarity on whatever projects we need to each week.

Meets weekly throughout the semester, Thursdays from 1-4pm. No meeting during Thanksgiving break.

title: Treasures of the Silk Road
location: McCalla Center, McCalla Center, 525 E. 9th Street, Bloomington, IN 47408
description:
The McCalla Center, in collaboration with musician and scholar Shahyar Daneshgar, celebrates the opening of its new exhibition Treasures of the Silk Road on Friday, September 25th, 4:00 pm-6:00 pm EDT.
The exhibit features over 70 musical instruments from the Pastel-Daneshgar musical instrument collection, with a focus on strings, flutes, and percussion from across Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa. Crafted from wood, snakeskin, horsehair, lambskin, camel bone, and other unique materials, these instruments provide a compelling history of cultural and artistic exchanges that have led to the myriad musical sounds and styles that permeate the world today. The opening event will feature remarks from the collection owner, Shahyar Daneshgar, and will feature musical clips provided by the Lotus World Music & Arts Festival.
Shahyar Daneshgar is a lifelong musician, scholar, and cultural ambassador whose passion for traditional music has shaped more than three decades of collecting, teaching, and performing. Born into a large musical family, he studied at the Tehran Conservatory of Music before pursuing academic work in Germany and later at Indiana University, where he earned his Ph.D. in Central Eurasian Studies in 1995. He taught at Indiana University until his retirement in 2024. He is founder and director of the Bloomington Silk Road Ensemble.
The exhibition is free and runs from September 25, 2026, to September 2027.
The mission of the McCalla Center is to provide accessible exhibition and educational experiences, creating opportunities for students, faculty, and the community to engage with collections, IU-generated creative activity, and community projects in meaningful and innovative ways.

title: Duo Cortona: Rachel Calloway, mezzo-soprano; Ari Streisfeld, violin Guest Recital
location: Ford-Crawford Hall, Simon Music Center, 200 S. Eagleson Ave, Bloomington, Indiana 47405
description:
Guest Recital
 Repertoire to be announced
 About the Artists
 Duo Cortona is a contemporary music ensemble dedicated to the creation of works for its unique instrumentation: mezzo-soprano and violin. This ensemble explores new sounds and possibilities for its intimate, expressive, and vital combination. Duo Cortona works to establish a new and thus far unexplored repertoire, pursuing the endless possibilities of this union. We create opportunities for both established and emerging composers through commissions, competitions, educational workshops, university residencies, and major concert performances. Duo Cortona was founded at the Cortona Sessions for New Music by husband and wife team Ari Streisfeld and Rachel Calloway. Recent and upcoming performances include the Southern Exposure Series for New Music, East Carolina New Music Initiative, University of Wisconsin, College of Charleston, New Music New College, the Gabriela Lena Frank Creative Academy of Music, Resonant Bodies Festival, The Stone, the SONiC Festival, New Music on the Point, and Contemporary Undercurrent of Song Project (Princeton).
 Mezzo-soprano Rachel Calloway brings versatility and compelling insight to stages worldwide. Praised as “a gale-force” (Time Out New York) with a “dark-hued and sizable voice” (New York Times), she is especially recognized as an interpreter of new and contemporary music. Recent and upcoming premieres include music by Augusta Read Thomas, John Zorn, Orlando Jacinto Garcia, Robert Xavier Rodriguez, David Garner, Gabriela Lena Frank, Christopher Cerrone, and Annika Socolofsky. Calloway has appeared in concert with the Orlando Philharmonic, Los Angeles Philharmonic New Music Series, Charleston Symphony, the New York Philharmonic, Berkeley Symphony, Ojai Festival, San Francisco Girls’ Chorus, BAM Next Wave Festival, Bridgehampton Chamber Music Festival, Cal Performances, and Lincoln Center Festival. Calloway made her European operatic debut as Mrs. Grose in The Turn of the Screw at Opéra de Reims, Athénée Théâtre Louis-Jovet (Paris), and Opéra de Lille. She cofounded the musical collective Shir Ami: Song of our People with her brother, cellist Jason Calloway. A passionate and devoted educator, Calloway serves on the faculty of the University of South Carolina as assistant professor of voice and director of Spark: Music Leadership at Carolina. She joined the faculty of the Cortona Sessions for New Music (Italy) in 2014, Summer Performing Arts with Juilliard in 2016, and the Chautauqua Opera Conservatory in 2023. Calloway earned degrees from The Juilliard School (B.M.) and Manhattan School of Music (M.M.).
 Violinist Ari Streisfeld has garnered critical acclaim worldwide for his performances of diverse repertoire and has established himself as one of the foremost interpreters of contemporary classical music. Praised for his “dazzling performance” by the New York Times and “scintillating playing” by New York Classical Review, Streisfeld is a founding member of the world renowned JACK Quartet. Recent season highlights include performances at Wigmore Hall (London), La Salle Pleyel (Paris), Teatro Colon (Argentina), Suntory Hall (Tokyo), Bali Arts Festival (Indonesia), Carriage Works (Sydney, Australia), Venice Biennale (Italy), Carnegie Hall, The Library of Congress, The Morgan Library (New York), the Lucerne Festival (Switzerland), and the Salzburg Festival (Austria). He has collaborated with many of today’s most prominent composers including John Luther Adams, Caroline Shaw, Julia Wolfe, Helmut Lachenmann, Matthias Pintscher, Georg Friedrich Haas, Steve Reich, and Salvatore Sciarrino. Streisfeld’s arrangements of madrigals and motets for string quartet by Machaut and Gesualdo have been performed to acclaim both at home and abroad. A recipient of the Morton Gould Young Composer Award, Streisfeld most recently premiered his Machaut arrangements for voice and violin at The Stone (New York). A passionate and committed music educator, Streisfeld serves on the faculty of New York’s Special Music School, Face the Music, New Music on the Point, and the Cortona Sessions for New Music (Italy). He is assistant professor of violin pedagogy at the University of South Carolina School of Music. Streisfeld attended the Eastman School of Music (Bachelor of Music), Northwestern University (Master of Music), and Boston University (Doctor of Musical Arts). He has recorded for Mode, Albany, Carrier, Innova, Canteloupe, and New World Records.

location: SIDNEY AND LOIS ESKENAZI MUSEUM OF ART
description: Highlighting a variety of works in the Eskenazi Museum of Art, including the Samuel Levi Jones: An Archeology of Knowledge exhibition, we'll consider sustainability beyond the environment and explore what we value—and hope for —in building a future for generations to come.About Your Guide  Blake Nietert is a Marketing, International, and Sustainable Business major with a minor in Art History. With five semesters of experience leading tours at the Eskenazi Museum of Art, he is slowly convincing himself that he has seen the artworks move when no one is watching.  While especially passionate about European art, Blake loves exploring and researching art from around the world. He finds that the Eskenazi Museum of Art always offers a new perspective on life when he needs it most. title: ACC's Over A Cup of Tea presents Aesthetics of the Cute: Globalization of East Asian Kawaii Culture by Haoxuan Gao
location: Asian Culture Center (807 E 10th street, Bloomington, IN)
description: From Hello Kitty's global empire to Labubu and K-pop idols, "cute" has become one of East Asia's most powerful and contested cultural exports. This session frames "cuteness" as an aesthetic category, tracing kawaii culture's root in postwar Japan, and its journey into global pop culture. A harder question follows: What gets flattened or fetishized when cuteness travels across cultures? This event will be facilitated by Haoxuan Gao, a Sociology PhD student at IU Bloomington who studies culture, modernity, and social psychology.      All Indiana University events, groups, activities, and educational, cultural, and historical observances welcome all IU students and other members of the Indiana University community.For more information, view this event in BeInvolved (https://beinvolved.indiana.edu/event/12476676).

title: First Thursday Declaration of Independence Lecture
description: As part of our yearlong America 250 programming, IU Associate Professor of History Konstantin Dierks will give a talk entitled "Resonances of the Declaration of Independence in American History."  Is it worth commemorating the Declaration of Independence in 2026? Does the Declaration still have resonance in our time of terrible crisis? The Declaration expressed ideals with intensely contested and severely limited meanings in 1776. Yet those brittle ideals somehow carried forward through American history. Looking closely at the complexities of 1776 can help us ponder how the Declaration might speak to our crisis in 2026.  Before and after the talk, please feel free to peruse our Declaration of Independence exhibitions: The Motives, The Moment and The Signers.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: Eric Andre: Subtle
location: The Comedy Attic, 123 S Walnut Street, Bloomington, IN
description: ERIC ANDRE is a comedian, actor and creator and host of Adult Swim’s hit series “The Eric Andre Show,” for which he won an Emmy Award.  He stars in the upcoming Netflix feature LITTLE BROTHER, directed by Matt Spicer, and recently appeared in HAPPY GILMORE 2 and Peter Farrelly’s BALLS UP.  In 2023, he was featured as an expert panelist on ABC’s “The Prank Panel,” alongside Johnny Knoxville and Gabourey Sidibe, and launched his first podcast “Bombing with Eric Andre” as part of the iHeartMedia and Will Ferrell’s Big Money Players Network. On the podcast, Andre asks his guest, usually a comedian or other type of performer, what their worst experience in front of an audience was, the worst bombing they’ve ever seen, and the most wasted they’ve ever been on stage. In 2022, Andre delivered a hilarious performance not to be missed in season two of HBO’s “The Righteous Gemstones” as ‘Lyle Lissons,’ a megachurch pastor from Texas who befriends Danny McBride’s ‘Jesse Gemstone.’   That same year, he also starred in an episode of the Netflix anthology series “Guillermo del Toro’s Cabinet of Curiosities.” In 2020, his first standup special “Legalize Everything” received critical praise when it premiered on Netflix and in 2021, he starred in the Netflix comedy BAD TRIP, which he produced and co-wrote with his director (Kitao Sakurai) from “The Eric Andre Show.” Co-starring Lil Rel Howery and Tiffany Haddish, the film was the #1 most viewed feature world-wide on the platform the first week of its release and marks a major moment in Andre’s career as it takes what he’s been doing with his comedy to the next level.   According to Howard Stern, “I believe this is gonna win an Academy Award.”  He added, “I was laughing so hard I thought my ribs might break.” Andre recently voiced ‘John Dory,’ the brother of Justin Timberlake’s ‘Branch’ in TROLLS BAND TOGETHER, as well as the demon ‘Luci’ on the Netflix animated series “Disenchantment” from creator Matt Groening.  He also lent his voice to the animated action comedy THE MITCHELLS VS. THE MACHINES, the animated feature SING 2, and the hyena ‘Azizi’ in Disney’s reimagining of THE LION KING, from director Jon Favreau. With an already proven standup act, Andre decided to break into the world of late-night talk shows. But, of course, he brings his own flare to what is otherwise a very organized and predictable late-night routine. Unlike his counterparts, Jimmy Fallon or Conan O’Brien, Andre’s unrelenting and constantly over the top humor puts some of his guests on “The Eric Andre Show” into situations they never thought they would end up in. “The Eric Andre Show” is a live-action-comedy television series that premiered in May 2012 on Cartoon Network’s Adult Swim. Andre was also seen on the big screen in ROUGH NIGHT, with Scarlett Johansson and Kate McKinnon.  His other film credits include POPSTAR: NEVER STOP NEVER STOPPING, with Andy Samberg, and THE INTERNSHIP, with Vince Vaughn and Owen Wilson. Andre starred on FXX’s “Man Seeking Woman” for three seasons from 2015 to 2017, with Jay Baruchel.  He was also a series regular on ABC’s “Don’t Trust the B---- in Apt. 23.”

title: SML & SML (XL)
description:
IU Jazz Studies, Jacobs School of Music, International Anthem Record Company, and Visit Bloomington Present: **SML**

**A quintet composed of luminaries from Los Angeles’s thriving jazz, improvised, and indie music scenes: bassist Anna Butterss (Jeff Parker, Jason Isbell, Phoebe Bridgers, Makaya McCraven), synthesist Jeremiah Chiu (Ariel Kalma, Marta Sofia Honer), saxophonist Josh Johnson (Meshell Ndegeocello, Flea, Leon Bridges, Carlos Niño), percussionist Booker Stardrum (Wendy Eisenberg, Horse Lords, Nels Cline) and guitarist Gregory Uhlmann (Sam Wilkes, Meg Duffy, Perfume Genius).**

Their debut album ***Small Medium Large*** was recorded at the band’s first gigs at Highland Park venue ETA in late 2022 and early 2023, post-produced in the following year, and released in Summer 2024 to wide critical acclaim, landing on ‘Best of 2024’ lists by Tone Glow, Passion of the Weiss, Bandcamp Daily, Hearing Things, and others. Following the release of *Small Medium Large*, the band quickly expanded beyond Los Angeles, performing at various festivals and venues and sharpening their sound. Recordings from these shows were then used as the basis for their sophomore album *HOW YOU BEEN*. This second release showcases a road-tested band pushing razor sharp confidence in the form of trance-inducing rhythm focused improvisation, but it also delves even deeper into the possibilities of post-production.

Upon its late-2025 release, ***HOW YOU BEEN*** was thoroughly praised by critics and fans alike, landing on numerous best of the year lists and even catching the attention of the *New York Times*, who published an in-depth feature on the band. The live shows that followed the album release had a similarly wide appeal, and support from well-credentialed outlets like NPR’s *World Cafe* have bolstered the fervent energy which has seen SML’s name recognition grow so quickly.

In March of 2026 SML held a residency at the **Big Ears Festival**, where the band played 6 sets over 3 nights to hundreds of fans, many of whom attended every show. The full, unedited SML experience is clearly of interest. In that spirit, ***Spontaneous Music Live***—an album of two unedited sidelong improvisations recorded at Zebulon in LA—was released in summer 2026, offering the first official recorded glimpse into the psychedelic realism and linear, hypnotic expansion of SML’s live sound.

There will be a 2nd set with **SML XL featuring John Raymond & Greg Ward.**

title: Ingrid Matthews, baroque violin
description: Repertoire and additional performers to be announcedAbout the ArtistIngrid Matthews teaches baroque violin in the Historical Performance Institute at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music. She served previously as music director of the Seattle Baroque Orchestra and has appeared as a soloist, guest director, and concertmaster for leading early music ensembles including the New York Collegium, Australian Brandenburg Orchestra, Boston Early Music Festival Orchestra, Ars Lyrica, Tafelmusik Baroque Orchestra, Musica Angelica, The Bach Sinfonia, Indianapolis Baroque Orchestra, and many others. She is also a member of San Francisco-based chamber ensemble Musica Pacifica and has held teaching residencies at the University of Southern California, University of Toronto, Oberlin College, Cornish College of the Arts, New England Conservatory, and others. First prizewinner in the 1989 Erwin Bodky International Competition for Early Music, Matthews herself has served as a juror for competitions such as the Maurice and Lillian Barbash International Bach Competition and the Indianapolis Early Music Competition. She has received high critical acclaim for her extensive discography; her recording of the Sonatas and Partitas for Unaccompanied Violin of J. S. Bach was named "top recommendation for this music...on either period or modern instruments" by American Record Guide, and her recording of Biagio Marini is included in the Norton Anthology of Music used by conservatories and universities worldwide.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Frances Lightbound: The Land Dissolves in Water | Exhibition
description: Lecture: October 27, 6:30–8pmExhibition: October 27–December 6, 2026, Mon.–Thur. 10am–4pm when IU classes are in session  Lightbound studies the production of space in urban environments, weaving narratives across photography, print, spatial interventions, and sculpture, with a focus on materials and sites in transition.  Architecture becomes an entry-point to questions of land use, ownership and access, bodily experience and perception, and timeframes ranging from the human to the geological. Lightbound invites viewers to consider and participate in the continual (re)construction of meaning in urban environments.  Frances Lightbound holds a B.A. from Glasgow School of Art, Scotland, and an M.F.A. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Recent solo exhibitions include Louise Hopkins Center for the Arts (Lubbock, TX), RULE Gallery (Marfa, TX), and the John David Mooney Foundation (Chicago, IL); her work has been exhibited internationally at venues in London, Glasgow and Berlin. Lightbound is a Lecturer at School of the Art Institute of Chicago in the departments of Print media and Photography.The J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program Lecture and Exhibition Series brings prominent working artists and architects to Columbus. Lectures take place in the auditorium and exhibitions in the gallery, both located within The Republic Building, 333 Second Street in Columbus. The gallery is open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. All events are free and open to the public.

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: ILJ Symposium: Evolving Frontiers in Criminal Law: Pregnancy, Family, and Identity
location: LOWELL E. BAIER HALL/IU MAURER SCHOOL OF LAW
description: The Symposium originated from the book, Pink Crime: Fighting Against the Criminalization of Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Queer Identity, authored by Professor Valena Beety, the Robert H. McKinney Professor of Law at Indiana University Maurer School of Law and a founding board member of the Indiana Innocence Project. Pink Crime focuses on the ways that criminal law is strategically used to limit the bodily autonomy of women and queer people, combined with a discussion of how the system as a whole targets the most vulnerable populations while allowing bias, stigma, and unreliable evidence to influence prosecution decisions, especially in situations where no crime occurred at all. As the book explores, the modern American legal system disproportionately punishes and often criminalizes identity, specifically in situations where pregnancy, motherhood, or queer identity are present.  This Symposium worked to expand upon Professor Beety's work in Pink Crime by bringing in additional perspectives to illustrate how existing and developing legal mechanisms strip away basic rights and lay the groundwork for more oppressive measures in the future. The Symposium convened a group of nationally-respected experts in wrongful convictions, criminal law, reproductive justice, family law, family policing, faulty forensics, gender law, and health law, among others. Their combined collection of work addressed emerging trends in prosecution, evidence, and punishment related to the topic.  This area of law is evolving too quickly for large portions of the legal academy to keep up. Importantly, this Symposium fills a gap in the existing legal scholarship. Discussions on pregnancy crime and gender affirming care are reaching the highest levels of state, national, and international governance, and informed scholarship is paramount as decisions continue to be made that affect massive amounts of individuals across the country, and even across the globe. Therefore, this Symposium aims to analyze the legal, social, and political dimensions of identity criminalization and provide timely theory, analysis, and practical solutions for professionals to draw on as we move forward.ILJ associates are required to attend at least two panels. Attendance will be taken.Schedule 9:00 – 10:00 AM Panel 1: The Prosecution of Pregnancy Behaviors and Outcomes10:15  11:15 AM Panel 2: Criminal Law After Dobbs11:30 AM – 12:30 PM Panel 3: Family Regulation Systems and Criminal Law2:00 – 3:00 PM Panel 4: Criminalizing Queer Life and Family3:15 – 4:15 PM Panel 5: Systemic Failures along the Path to Wrongful Convictions  Each of these five lectures has been approved for 1 hour of CLE credit by the Indiana Office of Admissions and Continuing Education.

title: Uncovering Our Past: VIRTUAL PROGRAM - "What Remains: The Monroe Reservoir Cemetery Relocation Project" (Monroe Lake)
location: Monroe Lake, VIRTUAL presentation at http://tinyurl.com/cemeteryrelocation2026
description:
Virtual Program: “What Remains: The Monroe Reservoir Cemetery Relocation Project” at 10:00 a.m.

This program will be presented LIVE on Facebook at tinyurl.com/cemeteryrelocation2026, with a question-and-answer session offered at the conclusion of the program. Mark yourself as “going” to receive a reminder about 10 minutes prior to the program’s start! If you are unable to view the program live, a recording will be available on the Reels tab of Monroe Lake’s Facebook page later in the day.

In 1960, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) was tasked with building a reservoir that would impact almost 50,000 acres in the Salt Creek Valley of south-central Indiana. This endeavor would necessitate the uprooting of thousands of people currently residing on the land. But it wasn’t just the living that had to be moved.

This is the story of how 7 cemeteries, consisting of 335 burials, were disinterred for the construction of Monroe Lake – and how they were reburied with the intent of preserving both cemetery history and family connections to the Salt Creek Valley. 

Please note that Monroe Lake has a public Facebook page. This means that a Facebook account is not required to watch either the live program or the recording; however, an account is required if you wish to ask questions or post comments on the video.

title: IKS Colloquium - Heangjin Park
description: IKS Fall 2026 Colloquium SeriesHeangjin Park  Department of Asian Languages and Cultures  University of Wisconsin-Madison  "Korean" Kimchi: A National, Global, and Diasporic CommodityFriday, November 612:00-1:00pmGISB 2067 | 355 N Eagleson Ave  How has kimchi, a fermented vegetable dish beloved by Koreans and beyond, become a national dish that symbolizes Korean culture? How has its Koreanness transformed through global production and circulation? And what does it mean for the Korean diaspora, who navigate political identity and economic opportunity from peripheral positions? This talk demonstrates how mundane commodities mediate the complex interplay among global capitalism, nationalism, and diasporic mobility across South Korea and China. Drawing on archival and ethnographic research into kimchi's commercial production and circulation, especially the Korean Chinese (chosonjok/chaoxianzu) kimchi business, this talk illuminates the political economic dynamics that reshape the multifaceted implications of "Korea."  Open to the public. A light lunch will be served.

title: Journal of Audiovisual Ethnomusicology Shorts Program | Additional Films and Guests
location: IU Cinema,1213 East 7th Street, Bloomington, IN 47406, USA
description:
This screening is a public rental presented by the Journal for Audiovisual Ethnomusicology (JAVEM), a peer-reviewed journal dedicated to audiovisual scholarship in ethnomusicology and related fields. Together, the three films demonstrate the range of audiovisual ethnomusicology across generations: from Hugo Zemp’s pioneering use of film as a tool for musical analysis, to Richard K. Wolf’s longitudinal and collaborative engagement with Kota musical and ritual life, to Matthew Machin-Autenrieth and Dario Ranocchiari’s exploration of music, history, and cultural memory in contemporary Granada.

The Song of Harmonics/Le chant des harmoniques (dir. Hugo Zemp, 1989, France): Made with ethnomusicologist and musician Trần Quang Hải, Hugo Zemp’s landmark film investigates overtone, or biphonic, singing, a technique in which a single singer produces a low fundamental while selectively emphasizing its harmonics to create a second audible melody. Moving between instruction, Mongolian khöömii performance, and scientific investigation, the film uses spectral and physiological imaging to make otherwise invisible aspects of vocal production visible. The Song of Harmonics is also an important example of ethnomusicological filmmaking in which audiovisual media function not simply to document musical practice, but as a method of research and analysis. This screening is presented in tribute to Hugo Zemp (1937–2026), a foundational figure in visual ethnomusicology, who passed away on January 3, 2026. [38 min; documentary; English and Mongolian]

Resonant Histories: Echoes of Al-Andalus in Granada (dir. Matthew Machin-Autenrieth and Dario Ranocchiari, 2026, Spain): Resonant Histories traces the complex relationship between Arab-Andalusian music and flamenco in Granada, a city where encounters between North African and Spanish musicians have long shaped musical life. Traveling through the streets of Sacromonte, closely associated with flamenco, and the Albaicín, Granada’s historic Arab quarter, the filmmakers draw on musicians, musicologists, historians, and local enthusiasts to explore the ways the city’s past continues to resonate in the present. The film moves from colonial exhibitions and early theatrical experiments combining Andalusí music and flamenco to Granada’s contemporary music scene, asking how histories of encounter, exchange, and representation are remembered—and continually remade—through musical practice. [59 min; documentary; Spanish with English subtitles]

Pots of Millet, Faces of Gold: Transformation (dir. Richard K. Wolf, 2025, India and USA): The first in a series of experimental ethnographic films drawing on Richard K. Wolf’s 35 years of research with the Kota people of South India’s Nilgiri Hills, Transformation explores a community of fewer than 2,500 people whose history has included disease, forced migration, and disruptions in the transmission of traditional knowledge. The film’s title evokes two poles of Kota ritual life: millet, central to multiday mortuary ceremonies, and gold-colored offerings fashioned as faces on the ancient pillars of Kota temples. Conceived as a time capsule addressed to Kota people 100 years in the future and narrated in Kota by Wolf’s longtime collaborator Duryodana, the film explores music alongside transformations of materials, bodies, and spiritual entities. It moves from pottery and musical-instrument making to their roles in mortuary ritual, combining Wolf’s footage from across decades with David G. Mandelbaum’s archival film and cylinder recordings from 1938 to create a layered portrait of Kota village life, historical change, and ethnographic encounter. [81 min; documentary; Kota and Tamil with English subtitles]

title: Treasures of the Silk Road
location: McCalla Center, McCalla Center, 525 E. 9th Street, Bloomington, IN 47408
description:
The McCalla Center, in collaboration with musician and scholar Shahyar Daneshgar, celebrates the opening of its new exhibition Treasures of the Silk Road on Friday, September 25th, 4:00 pm-6:00 pm EDT.
The exhibit features over 70 musical instruments from the Pastel-Daneshgar musical instrument collection, with a focus on strings, flutes, and percussion from across Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa. Crafted from wood, snakeskin, horsehair, lambskin, camel bone, and other unique materials, these instruments provide a compelling history of cultural and artistic exchanges that have led to the myriad musical sounds and styles that permeate the world today. The opening event will feature remarks from the collection owner, Shahyar Daneshgar, and will feature musical clips provided by the Lotus World Music & Arts Festival.
Shahyar Daneshgar is a lifelong musician, scholar, and cultural ambassador whose passion for traditional music has shaped more than three decades of collecting, teaching, and performing. Born into a large musical family, he studied at the Tehran Conservatory of Music before pursuing academic work in Germany and later at Indiana University, where he earned his Ph.D. in Central Eurasian Studies in 1995. He taught at Indiana University until his retirement in 2024. He is founder and director of the Bloomington Silk Road Ensemble.
The exhibition is free and runs from September 25, 2026, to September 2027.
The mission of the McCalla Center is to provide accessible exhibition and educational experiences, creating opportunities for students, faculty, and the community to engage with collections, IU-generated creative activity, and community projects in meaningful and innovative ways.

description: For painter Michael Berryhill, there's no difference between realism and abstraction. His work reminds the viewer of the challenge of capturing the process of painting, and the physical and conceptual layering that a surface might contain.Berryhill has had solo exhibitions at Night Gallery in Los Angeles and at both Kate Werble and Derek Eller galleries in New York City and been reviewed in The New York Times, Hyperallergic, Art in America, Artforum, The Brooklyn Rail, Modern Painters, Huffington Post, Time Out NY, Artnet News, Flaunt magazine,Whitehot Magazine of Contemporary Art, L Magazine, and artcritical.Berryhill earned his M.F.A. from Columbia University and has held visiting faculty positions at Bard, Columbia, Pratt, and VCU. Berryhill was Dean of Skowhegan School of Painting and Sculpture for two years. He was artist-in-residence at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville and Virginia Commonwealth University in Richmond, Virginia and held the Painting's Edge Residency at Idyllwild Arts Academy in California. He received a New York Foundation for the Arts Fellowship for Painting and was a Studio Space recipient at the Marie Walsh Sharpe Art Foundation.Born in El Paso, Texas, Michael Berryhill earned his undergraduate degree at University of Texas Austin. He lives and works in Ellenville, New York.Artist's instagram:  @berryhillmichael

title: Eric Andre: Subtle
location: The Comedy Attic, 123 S Walnut Street, Bloomington, IN
description: ERIC ANDRE is a comedian, actor and creator and host of Adult Swim’s hit series “The Eric Andre Show,” for which he won an Emmy Award.  He stars in the upcoming Netflix feature LITTLE BROTHER, directed by Matt Spicer, and recently appeared in HAPPY GILMORE 2 and Peter Farrelly’s BALLS UP.  In 2023, he was featured as an expert panelist on ABC’s “The Prank Panel,” alongside Johnny Knoxville and Gabourey Sidibe, and launched his first podcast “Bombing with Eric Andre” as part of the iHeartMedia and Will Ferrell’s Big Money Players Network. On the podcast, Andre asks his guest, usually a comedian or other type of performer, what their worst experience in front of an audience was, the worst bombing they’ve ever seen, and the most wasted they’ve ever been on stage. In 2022, Andre delivered a hilarious performance not to be missed in season two of HBO’s “The Righteous Gemstones” as ‘Lyle Lissons,’ a megachurch pastor from Texas who befriends Danny McBride’s ‘Jesse Gemstone.’   That same year, he also starred in an episode of the Netflix anthology series “Guillermo del Toro’s Cabinet of Curiosities.” In 2020, his first standup special “Legalize Everything” received critical praise when it premiered on Netflix and in 2021, he starred in the Netflix comedy BAD TRIP, which he produced and co-wrote with his director (Kitao Sakurai) from “The Eric Andre Show.” Co-starring Lil Rel Howery and Tiffany Haddish, the film was the #1 most viewed feature world-wide on the platform the first week of its release and marks a major moment in Andre’s career as it takes what he’s been doing with his comedy to the next level.   According to Howard Stern, “I believe this is gonna win an Academy Award.”  He added, “I was laughing so hard I thought my ribs might break.” Andre recently voiced ‘John Dory,’ the brother of Justin Timberlake’s ‘Branch’ in TROLLS BAND TOGETHER, as well as the demon ‘Luci’ on the Netflix animated series “Disenchantment” from creator Matt Groening.  He also lent his voice to the animated action comedy THE MITCHELLS VS. THE MACHINES, the animated feature SING 2, and the hyena ‘Azizi’ in Disney’s reimagining of THE LION KING, from director Jon Favreau. With an already proven standup act, Andre decided to break into the world of late-night talk shows. But, of course, he brings his own flare to what is otherwise a very organized and predictable late-night routine. Unlike his counterparts, Jimmy Fallon or Conan O’Brien, Andre’s unrelenting and constantly over the top humor puts some of his guests on “The Eric Andre Show” into situations they never thought they would end up in. “The Eric Andre Show” is a live-action-comedy television series that premiered in May 2012 on Cartoon Network’s Adult Swim. Andre was also seen on the big screen in ROUGH NIGHT, with Scarlett Johansson and Kate McKinnon.  His other film credits include POPSTAR: NEVER STOP NEVER STOPPING, with Andy Samberg, and THE INTERNSHIP, with Vince Vaughn and Owen Wilson. Andre starred on FXX’s “Man Seeking Woman” for three seasons from 2015 to 2017, with Jay Baruchel.  He was also a series regular on ABC’s “Don’t Trust the B---- in Apt. 23.”

title: University Orchestra – Camilo Téllez, alumnus guest conductor
description: Repertoire  Milhaud: Le bœuf sur la toit, Op. 58 (1919)Gabriela Lena Frank: Elegía andina (2000)Piazzolla: Sinfonietta (1953)Sibelius: Suite from "Pelleas and Melisande," Op. 46 (1905)About the Conductor  Conductor Camilo Téllez is director of orchestras for the Community School at the Colburn School. His artistic development was shaped within the Los Angeles Philharmonic and the Dudamel Fellowship (2021-22), where he worked closely with Gustavo Dudamel, collaborating with artists such as Zubin Mehta, Michael Tilson Thomas, Elim Chan, Hilary Hahn, Beatrice Rana, Emanuel Ax, and María Dueñas. His work has taken him across the United States, Europe, Latin America, and China, with appearances including the Los Angeles Philharmonic, the Bogotá Philharmonic Orchestra, the Naples Philharmonic, the Florida Orchestra, the Netherlands Philharmonic Orchestra, the Hamburg Theater Orchestra, and the Turku Chamber Orchestra. His artistic practice includes a 30-city tour in China, as well as collaborations in diverse performance contexts, including a production of Peter and the Wolf at the Hollywood Bowl, featuring narrator Viola Davis, and a production of Fidelio involving deaf performers, under Gustavo Dudamel. He has also participated in performances of rediscovered repertoire, including a lost violin concerto by African-Cuban composer Joseph White, performed with violinist Rachel Barton Pine. Téllez has developed a deep passion for inspiring and mentoring younger generations of musicians through orchestral training and music education. He believes that orchestras are a reflection of a complex society, where discipline, empathy, collaboration, and mutual respect can shape not only better musicians but also better human beings. This philosophy has guided his extensive experience working with youth orchestras, festivals, universities, and educational programs throughout the United States, China, Venezuela, Colombia, and Panama, collaborating with youth, university, and community ensembles. As instrumentalist, he maintains an active study of the organ, with a focus on the music of Bach and Buxtehude, which informs his understanding of structure, sound, and orchestral color. He earned a Master of Music degree in Orchestral Conducting from the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music and a Bachelor of Music from Juan N. Corpas in Colombia.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Frances Lightbound: The Land Dissolves in Water | Exhibition
description: Lecture: October 27, 6:30–8pmExhibition: October 27–December 6, 2026, Mon.–Thur. 10am–4pm when IU classes are in session  Lightbound studies the production of space in urban environments, weaving narratives across photography, print, spatial interventions, and sculpture, with a focus on materials and sites in transition.  Architecture becomes an entry-point to questions of land use, ownership and access, bodily experience and perception, and timeframes ranging from the human to the geological. Lightbound invites viewers to consider and participate in the continual (re)construction of meaning in urban environments.  Frances Lightbound holds a B.A. from Glasgow School of Art, Scotland, and an M.F.A. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Recent solo exhibitions include Louise Hopkins Center for the Arts (Lubbock, TX), RULE Gallery (Marfa, TX), and the John David Mooney Foundation (Chicago, IL); her work has been exhibited internationally at venues in London, Glasgow and Berlin. Lightbound is a Lecturer at School of the Art Institute of Chicago in the departments of Print media and Photography.The J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program Lecture and Exhibition Series brings prominent working artists and architects to Columbus. Lectures take place in the auditorium and exhibitions in the gallery, both located within The Republic Building, 333 Second Street in Columbus. The gallery is open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. All events are free and open to the public.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: Aanikoobijigan w/ Q&A | Additional Films and Guests
location: IU Cinema,1213 East 7th Street, Bloomington, IN 47406, USA
description:
"What's the difference between an archaeologist and a grave robber?" an elder asks. "A degree," he laughs. Aanikoobijigan examines the ongoing struggle to repatriate Indigenous ancestors' remains from museums and archives, exposing the thin line between archaeology and grave robbery. With striking visuals and grounded Indigenous perspectives, Aanikoobijigan challenges institutional resistance to decolonization and affirms that returning ancestors to the earth restores memory, dignity, and balance, reminding us that no community can be whole until their ancestors are finally laid to rest. [80 min; documentary; English and Anishinaabemowin with English subtitles]

The screening will be followed by a conversation between IU Indianapolis professor Dr. Holly Cusack-McVeigh (Anthropology and Museum Studies; Public Scholar of Collections and Community Curation)—who is featured in the film—and Dr. Olof Olafardottir-Hamilton (Assistant Director, Office of the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act, Indiana University).

title: Uncovering Our Past: Southern Indiana Folk Songs, Paynetown SRA (Monroe Lake)
location: Monroe Lake, Paynetown SRA, Activity Center
description:
Southern Indiana Folk Songs at 6:00 p.m.

•    Free program (donations accepted) and free park entry!
•    Location: Paynetown State Recreation Area, Activity Center
•    Please note that seating is limited to 25 people; we don’t expect the room to fill, but we could always be surprised!

Folk songs proliferated in an era when singing was a common form of recreation. People learned traditional folk songs by listening to others sing them and then passing them on to someone else. The Salt Creek Valley, where Monroe Lake now lies, has a rich history of song, heavily influenced by the people who moved here in the 1800s from the Appalachian region. This program explores the history of folk music in southern Indiana and songs once sung right here in the valley, including audio recordings of local singers from the 1930s through 1980s.
